Title: Ventilator allocation during a surge
Description: A hospital has fewer ventilators than patients who need them. Some are more likely to survive with treatment, while others have waited longer or are more seriously ill. A triage team must choose whether to prioritize expected survival or give equal chances among eligible patients.
Utilitarianism: Survival differences matter when one machine cannot serve everyone. Directing ventilators toward patients most likely to recover preserves more lives from the same scarce resource. When prognoses are genuinely similar, a lottery avoids wasting effort on distinctions that change no outcome.
Deontology: Scarcity does not erase equal moral status. Criteria may consider medical need and whether treatment can work, but not social worth. Patients with comparable clinical claims should receive the same chance rather than being ranked by whose life appears more valuable.
Virtue Ethics: Scarcity puts judgment under public pressure. A hospital that hides subjective preference behind clinical language loses integrity. A sound team uses prognosis where it truly matters, admits uncertainty openly, and refuses to let panic turn difficult choices into favoritism.
Care Ethics: Being denied ventilation does not end a patient's claim on the hospital. Communication, symptom relief, and family contact should continue for those without the machine. A defensible triage process leaves the bonds of care intact even while scarce resources are distributed unequally.
Sources: Emanuel EJ et al. (2020), “Fair Allocation of Scarce Medical Resources in the Time of Covid-19,” New England Journal of Medicine. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32202722/

Title: ICU priority and vaccination status
Description: An intensive care unit is full during an infectious disease surge. Two patients need the next bed and have similar clinical prospects, but one declined a widely available preventive vaccine. The triage team must decide whether that earlier choice should reduce the unvaccinated patient's priority.
Utilitarianism: Earlier refusal matters only through its effects now. Giving some priority to the vaccinated patient can protect incentives, reward risk reduction, and reduce future pressure on scarce beds. With otherwise similar prospects, those wider consequences support modestly lower priority for voluntary nonvaccination.
Deontology: Emergency treatment is not a reward for previous obedience. Once two patients have comparable medical claims, lowering one person's priority because of a past refusal turns care into punishment. Allocation should rely on present clinical criteria, not moral judgment about earlier choices.
Virtue Ethics: Past refusal can easily become a reason for moral contempt. A hospital that lets resentment shape rescue becomes punitive rather than clinical. Prevention can be promoted firmly beforehand without allowing dislike of earlier choices to decide who receives care during crisis.
Care Ethics: Once illness brings someone into intensive care, the earlier vaccine decision sits inside a new relation of dependence and need. That history may shape conversation, but equal bedside concern should remain unless treating one patient would directly endanger another.
Sources: Shaw D. (2022), “Vaccination status and intensive care unit triage: Is it fair to give unvaccinated Covid-19 patients equal priority?” Bioethics. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9538027/

Title: Withholding a terminal diagnosis
Description: A physician learns that a patient has a terminal illness. The family asks that the diagnosis be hidden because they fear the truth will destroy the patient's hope. The physician must decide whether to disclose the prognosis directly or follow the family's request for nondisclosure.
Utilitarianism: Truth can cause immediate distress, but it also enables treatment choices, financial planning, farewells, and symptom decisions. Those benefits usually outweigh temporary protection from bad news. The physician should disclose the diagnosis sensitively while checking how much detail the patient wants.
Deontology: The diagnosis belongs first to the patient whose body and choices are affected. Hiding material information prevents informed decisions and treats the family as the rightful controller of another adult's life. Unless the patient previously asked not to know, disclosure is required.
Virtue Ethics: A terminal diagnosis makes avoidance tempting because silence can look compassionate. A physician who hides the truth to escape distress abandons honesty. Better practice stays present, speaks plainly without cruelty, and accepts the emotional burden that truthful care creates.
Care Ethics: Family protection and clinical trust pull in different directions here. The relatives' fear should not be dismissed, yet the patient depends on an honest relationship with the physician. Preparing a gentle disclosure together protects both connections better than secrecy or confrontation.
Sources: McCabe MS et al. (2010), “When the Family Requests Withholding the Diagnosis: Who Owns the Truth?” Journal of Oncology Practice. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2835490/

Title: Refusal of a life-saving amputation
Description: A patient with spreading infection will die without amputation of his leg. He is fully competent, understands this, and refuses, saying he would rather die whole than live dependent. His family begs the surgeon to operate anyway. The surgeon must amputate or accept refusal.
Utilitarianism: Overriding a competent refusal saves this leg and this life, and teaches every future patient that stated wishes can be set aside when doctors disagree. That loss of trust costs more lives than it saves. Accept the refusal.
Deontology: His body is not the surgeon's to improve. A competent refusal is binding whatever it costs, and the family's distress, however real, gives them no claim over what is done to him. Do not operate.
Virtue Ethics: Rescue feels like the whole of medicine when a man is dying. But a surgeon who cannot bear to be refused has made the patient's body an extension of his own competence. Restraint is the harder discipline.
Care Ethics: He is not refusing help; he is refusing a particular future. The surgeon can stay with him, treat the pain, and sit with a family who will need somewhere to put their grief. That is still care.
Sources: Beauchamp TL & Childress JF (2019), Principles of Biomedical Ethics, 8th ed., Oxford University Press, chapter on respect for autonomy. VERIFY EDITION AND PAGE.

Title: Genetic risk disclosure to relatives
Description: A patient learns of an inherited condition that gives close relatives a serious preventable health risk. The patient refuses to tell them and asks the clinician to keep the result private. The clinician must decide whether confidentiality should hold or whether relatives should be warned.
Utilitarianism: Preventable serious illness in several relatives can outweigh the harm of a limited confidentiality breach. After strong efforts to persuade the patient, warning those at substantial risk prevents more harm than it causes when effective prevention or early treatment is genuinely available.
Deontology: Confidentiality is a promise attached to clinical trust, but duties can conflict when silence exposes identifiable people to serious avoidable harm. Disclosure becomes defensible only as an exceptional, minimal breach after persuasion fails, not as routine sharing of family-relevant information.
Virtue Ethics: Familial risk turns loyalty in more than one direction. Rushing to disclose becomes careless with trust, while hiding behind confidentiality can become evasive. Mature judgment presses hard for voluntary sharing and treats breach as a reluctant last resort.
Care Ethics: Genetic information links the patient to relatives who may share the same risk. Silence protects one bond while leaving another person unknowingly exposed. Working toward voluntary disclosure preserves trust while still recognizing the relatives' dependence on information they cannot obtain alone.
Sources: Lucassen A, Clarke A. (2021), “In the family: access to, and communication of, familial information in clinical practice,” Human Genetics. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00439-021-02401-0

Title: Biased diagnostic AI
Description: A hospital uses software that helps identify disease from patient records. Audits show that it performs well overall but misses more cases in one minority group. Leaders must decide whether to keep using it with human review or suspend it until performance is improved.
Utilitarianism: Removing a useful tool also causes missed diagnoses, so total diagnostic performance cannot be ignored. Keeping it with mandatory review for the affected group preserves much of its benefit while reducing unequal harm. Suspension is better if that safeguard cannot close the gap.
Deontology: Patients are entitled to the same standard of diagnostic attention regardless of group membership. A known error pattern cannot be accepted merely because averages look good. Continued use requires a safeguard that gives affected patients an equivalent opportunity for accurate assessment.
Virtue Ethics: Unequal error rates tempt leaders to hide behind a strong average score. Once they know who is being missed, continuing unchanged says that impressive performance matters more than repair. Responsible use makes correction visible instead of treating bias as acceptable collateral.
Care Ethics: Diagnostic mistakes fall repeatedly on patients who cannot repair the system themselves. Human review should follow that group closely, with clinicians responsible for noticing when the tool fails. Continued use is acceptable only if that protection remains genuinely reliable.
Sources: Hussain SA, Bresnahan M, Zhuang J. (2024), “The bias algorithm: how AI in healthcare exacerbates ethnic and racial disparities – a scoping review,” Ethnicity & Health. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39488857/

Title: Request for assisted dying
Description: A competent patient with terminal illness has severe suffering despite ongoing treatment and asks a physician for medical help to end life. The practice is legally available under safeguards. The physician must decide whether to participate or continue symptom-focused care without providing life-ending medication.
Utilitarianism: When suffering is severe, persistent, and chosen safeguards make coercion unlikely, assisting death can prevent more harm than prolonging an unwanted dying process. On the facts given, participation is favored if alternatives have been discussed and the patient's request remains stable.
Deontology: A physician's authority to treat does not automatically include permission to intentionally help cause death. Even voluntary suffering has limits on what one person may do to another. The physician should continue palliation and support without providing means for a life-ending act.
Virtue Ethics: Severe suffering tests what healing means when cure is gone. Automatic refusal can become moral distance, while automatic agreement can reduce healing to relief alone. The physician must face the request directly and decide whether participation fits a humane professional identity.
Care Ethics: End-of-life dependence reaches beyond the patient's request. Family pressure, exhaustion, isolation, and untreated symptoms can all shape what choice feels available. If strong support addresses those pressures and the wish remains stable, respecting it may preserve rather than abandon the relationship.
Sources: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2018), “Physician-Assisted Death: Scanning the Landscape,” Chapter 2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK525943/

Title: When a family cannot pay
Description: A woman needs surgery that her family cannot afford. The hospital can waive the fee, but its charity budget is small and other patients will need it later. Delay makes her condition worse. The surgeon must waive the fee now or hold the funds.
Utilitarianism: A budget spent on the first person who asks helps fewer people than one spent where each unit of aid buys most. Holding funds is defensible only if a real system for deciding later cases exists; without one, treat her now.
Deontology: Ability to pay is not a medical fact and cannot decide who receives care that is clinically indicated. A hospital holding funds against hypothetical future patients owes an account to the actual patient in front of it now.
Virtue Ethics: Money makes it easy to call refusal prudence. Watch whether the surgeon is protecting the fund or protecting himself from a hard conversation, and whether the hospital's stewardship has quietly become a habit of saying no.
Care Ethics: She came to this hospital, not to a future one. The people who will need the fund later have no face and no relationship here, while she and her family are already known to this team. Treat her.
Sources: Xu K et al. (2003), “Household catastrophic health expenditure: a multicountry analysis,” The Lancet 362(9378). VERIFY LINK.

Title: Disability in scarce-bed allocation
Description: A hospital has one intensive care bed for two patients with similar chances of surviving the immediate illness. One has a long-term disability that may reduce independence after recovery. The team must decide whether predicted future quality of life should influence who receives the bed.
Utilitarianism: Future health can matter when scarce treatment creates very different amounts of benefit. Yet broad disability labels predict lived wellbeing poorly and risk systematic error. With similar survival prospects, that uncertainty outweighs the claimed gain, so disability should not lower priority.
Deontology: A disability does not reduce a person's claim to lifesaving treatment. Ranking patients by predicted independence turns equal persons into estimates of desirable lives. Unless the disability directly changes whether treatment can work, it must not count against access to the bed.
Virtue Ethics: Quality-of-life scoring can quietly redefine which lives a hospital admires. Once independence becomes a measure of worth, social preference can masquerade as medicine. A decent hospital resists that drift and keeps scarcity decisions tied directly to whether treatment can work.
Care Ethics: A quality score can erase the disabled patient's existing ties, adaptations, and ordinary life. Equal clinical priority better holds that person in view of the team, rather than replacing them with an outsider's prediction about independence and a supposedly diminished future.
Sources: Göttert EAF. (2025), “What is fair? Ethical analysis of triage criteria and disability rights during the COVID-19 pandemic and the German legislation,” Journal of Medical Ethics. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37973368/

Title: Kidney allocation by benefit or waiting
Description: One donor kidney is available for two medically suitable patients. One has waited much longer, while the other is expected to gain more years of healthy kidney function. The transplant team must use a rule giving greater weight either to waiting time or expected benefit.
Utilitarianism: A transplant that functions longer creates more health from one irreplaceable organ. Expected benefit should carry greater weight when the difference is substantial, while waiting time can break close cases. Giving the kidney where it is likely to work longest preserves benefit.
Deontology: Years already spent waiting create a claim that cannot be ignored whenever another patient promises more benefit. A legitimate rule must be public, consistent, and protect equal access. Expected outcome may matter, but it cannot erase fair consideration of time already borne.
Virtue Ethics: One donor organ can turn stewardship into obsession with efficiency. A responsible transplant system uses the kidney well without forgetting people who waited under its rules. The better policy resists both mechanical seniority and the arrogance of treating predicted longevity as everything.
Care Ethics: Long waiting changes families and patients through dialysis routines, dependence, and uncertainty. The other patient also has a future at stake. A humane allocation rule keeps those lived burdens visible alongside expected medical benefit instead of treating either side as abstract.
Sources: HRSA/OPTN Ethics Committee, “Ethical Principles in the Allocation of Human Organs.” https://www.hrsa.gov/optn/professionals/resources/ethical-considerations/ethical-principles-in-the-allocation-of-human-organs

Title: Involuntary psychiatric admission
Description: A psychiatric patient says they may seriously harm themselves but refuses hospital admission. Involuntary admission could protect them during crisis, yet it removes liberty and may damage future trust. The psychiatrist must decide whether to admit without consent or continue voluntary community support.
Utilitarianism: A temporary loss of liberty is outweighed by preventing a highly probable death or severe injury. Given an immediate serious risk, short involuntary admission is the safer course on the numbers, provided restrictions end when the crisis passes and treatment actively restores voluntary participation.
Deontology: Liberty cannot be removed merely because clinicians believe another choice would be wiser. Coercion becomes permissible only when capacity or imminent danger meets a clear legal and ethical threshold. If that threshold is met, the restriction must remain necessary, proportionate, and reviewable.
Virtue Ethics: Immediate danger gives coercion a powerful justification and therefore a special risk of misuse. The psychiatrist should neither romanticize autonomy nor confine from fear. Sound judgment uses force reluctantly, explains it honestly, and works to return control as soon as possible.
Care Ethics: Forced admission can preserve life while damaging the patient's trust in the people providing treatment. If coercion is necessary, explanation, contact with trusted people, and a clear path back to voluntary care become part of preserving the relationship rather than optional additions.
Sources: Laureano CD, Laranjeira C, Querido A, Dixe MA, Rego F. (2024), “Ethical Issues in Clinical Decision-Making about Involuntary Psychiatric Treatment: A Scoping Review,” Healthcare. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38391820/

Title: Consent to join a trial
Description: A trial offers a patient a drug that might help when standard treatment has failed. He is very unwell, trusts his doctor, and agrees quickly without reading much. His doctor is also the investigator. She must enrol him now or arrange independent counselling first.
Utilitarianism: Trials that recruit slowly answer their question late, and every month of delay leaves the next patients without evidence. But consent obtained under trust that later collapses damages recruitment far more. Arrange the independent conversation; it costs a day.
Deontology: Agreement given because a trusted doctor asked is not the same as agreement given knowing what is being asked. When the person seeking consent also benefits from obtaining it, someone else must do the asking.
Virtue Ethics: The quick yes is the tempting part. A doctor who wants the trial to succeed will find his patient's eagerness convincing, and will not notice himself deciding what the patient wants. Honesty here means doubting your own reading.
Care Ethics: He is agreeing to the person, not to the protocol. That trust is the good thing in the room and the reason it cannot be used. Bringing in someone with nothing at stake protects what he actually values here.
Sources: World Medical Association, Declaration of Helsinki: Ethical Principles for Medical Research Involving Human Subjects. Also Appelbaum PS et al. (1982), “The therapeutic misconception,” International Journal of Law and Psychiatry. VERIFY LINKS.

Title: Priority for protective equipment
Description: A hospital has too little protective equipment during an outbreak. Giving the best supplies first to frontline staff may keep care functioning, but patients and support workers also face exposure. Leaders must choose whether clinical staff receive priority or equipment follows immediate risk alone.
Utilitarianism: Protecting workers who can then treat many others multiplies the benefit of each scarce item. Frontline clinical staff should receive some priority when exposure and replacement difficulty are high, because keeping them healthy protects future patients and hospital functioning.
Deontology: Priority cannot rest on professional prestige. It is justified only by role-based exposure and obligations the institution created by asking people to face danger. Workers with comparable risk deserve comparable protection, including support staff, regardless of whether their job carries clinical status.
Virtue Ethics: Protective shortages expose whether praise for frontline workers is matched by real responsibility. Calling people heroes while leaving them unprotected turns admiration into an excuse. Leaders should protect those carrying greatest exposure without treating less visible workers as expendable.
Care Ethics: Scarce protective equipment links patients, nurses, cleaners, and families through shared exposure. Patients rely on staff staying healthy; workers rely on the hospital not to abandon them. Priority should follow those lines of dependence rather than a narrow hierarchy of professional status.
Sources: WHO, “Coronavirus disease (COVID-19): Ethics, resource allocation and priority setting.” https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/coronavirus-disease-covid-19-ethics-resource-allocation-and-priority-setting

Title: Experimental treatment for a child
Description: A child with a terminal illness may qualify for an experimental treatment with uncertain benefit and serious risks. One parent wants to proceed while the other refuses. The clinical team must decide whether to delay for agreement or seek authorization to begin despite the disagreement.
Utilitarianism: Delay may remove the only remaining chance of benefit, but an unproven treatment can add suffering without extending life. With substantial uncertainty and divided parents, urgent ethics review is preferable unless clinicians have strong evidence that waiting will close the treatment window.
Deontology: Parents normally exercise authority together for a child, and neither preference can simply be ignored when treatment is highly uncertain. Overriding disagreement requires a child-protection justification based on clear risk or benefit, not the team's belief that one parent seems more reasonable.
Virtue Ethics: An experimental option can make action look braver than restraint. The team should resist rescue at any cost and avoidance of controversy alike. Its response should show that uncertainty is faced honestly, with neither parental fear nor medical ambition deciding by itself.
Care Ethics: Parental conflict surrounds a child who depends on everyone involved. Before turning disagreement into a legal contest, the team should help both parents understand the child's suffering, hopes, and limits together, unless delay itself threatens the remaining treatment chance.
Sources: Barone S, Unguru Y. (2018), “Ethical Issues Around Pediatric Death: Navigating Consent, Assent, and Disagreement Regarding Life-Sustaining Medical Treatment,” Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Clinics of North America. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30219216/

Title: Reporting a contagious disease
Description: A patient is diagnosed with a serious contagious disease and asks the physician not to report it, fearing stigma and job loss. Public health rules require notification so exposed people can be protected. The physician must choose confidentiality or report despite the patient's objection.
Utilitarianism: Silent confidentiality leaves other people exposed to preventable infection. Reporting produces the better outcome when notification enables testing, treatment, or outbreak control. The physician should disclose only what authorities need and reduce avoidable harm to the patient from stigma or employment consequences.
Deontology: Confidentiality is important but never an unconditional promise against lawful public-health duties. When reporting is required to protect others from serious communicable harm, the physician must comply while limiting disclosure to the necessary information and informing the patient whenever possible.
Virtue Ethics: Legal reporting can turn a clinician into either a secret keeper or an impersonal agent of authority. A trustworthy physician avoids both roles, reports what is required, explains the decision directly, and does not let compliance become indifference to the patient's fear.
Care Ethics: Mandatory reporting protects strangers but may leave this patient exposed socially and economically. The clinical relationship should continue through help with disclosure, treatment, work concerns, and contact tracing, so public protection does not become abandonment of the person who first sought care.
Sources: AMA Code of Medical Ethics, Opinion 3.2.1, “Confidentiality.” https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/confidentiality

Title: Operating without a referral option
Description: A patient at a rural clinic needs an operation the single doctor there has performed only twice, under supervision. The nearest hospital that can do it is eight hours away and the patient may not survive the journey. The doctor must operate or send him.
Utilitarianism: Compare two survival estimates, not one. An inexperienced operation carries real risk, but so does eight hours in transit for someone unstable. Where the transfer is more likely to kill him than the surgery, operating is the better bet.
Deontology: A doctor may not practise beyond competence, but the duty not to abandon a patient does not lapse because help is far away. If he operates, the patient must know what he is consenting to: an inexperienced surgeon or a long road.
Virtue Ethics: Two failures sit either side of this. Refusing out of fear for his record leaves a man to die on a road; operating to prove something risks a life for pride. Courage here looks like an honest estimate of his own hands.
Care Ethics: Sending him away is not neutral. It moves him from the one clinician who knows him to a journey with no one, and his family cannot follow. Whatever is decided, he should not travel those hours alone.
Sources: Meara JG et al. (2015), “Global Surgery 2030: evidence and solutions for achieving health, welfare, and economic development,” The Lancet 386(9993). VERIFY LINK.

Title: Patient data for commercial AI
Description: A hospital is offered a partnership with a technology company seeking de-identified patient records to develop diagnostic software. The project could improve future care, but patients did not specifically agree to commercial use. Leaders must decide whether to share the data or seek permission first.
Utilitarianism: A useful diagnostic system could benefit many patients, but a partnership that surprises current patients can damage trust and future participation. Seeking explicit permission is preferable when feasible, because the delay costs less than treating clinical records as commercial assets by default.
Deontology: Removing names does not erase the question of who authorized commercial use. Information was given in a clinical relationship for care, not automatically for outside product development. The hospital should obtain permission or use a governance basis patients were entitled to expect.
Virtue Ethics: A commercial offer can turn entrusted information into an attractive commercial asset. Quietly stretching existing permission makes innovation opportunistic. A trustworthy hospital explains the arrangement before benefiting from it and accepts refusal without allowing that choice to affect clinical care.
Care Ethics: Clinical records came from encounters in which patients depended on the hospital for treatment. Turning those records into a commercial dataset changes that relationship after names are removed. Seeking permission draws patients into what happens to information produced through their dependence.
Sources: AMA Code of Medical Ethics, Opinion 3.2.4, “Access to Medical Records by Data Collection Companies.” https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/confidentiality-electronic-medical-records

Title: Placebo without full disclosure
Description: A physician treats chronic pain that has not improved with standard options. A placebo may reduce symptoms, but the physician believes it will work better if described as active treatment. The choice is deceptive prescribing or an openly disclosed placebo that may work less well.
Utilitarianism: Deception may strengthen an immediate placebo response, but damaged trust can affect later treatment decisions. Because open-label placebos can still help some patients, transparent use offers much of the benefit without the broader cost of discovering deliberate physician deception.
Deontology: A physician cannot secure therapeutic cooperation by giving false information about what is being prescribed. Informed consent requires truthful explanation even when deception might improve symptoms. An openly disclosed placebo is permissible; presenting it as an active drug is not.
Virtue Ethics: A placebo makes helpful deception seem small and practical. Once misleading a patient becomes normal whenever it appears useful, professional honesty turns conditional. Open prescribing keeps therapeutic creativity without teaching the physician to treat trust as another instrument.
Care Ethics: Chronic pain makes trust in the physician especially important because relief has already been difficult to find. A hidden placebo could turn that dependence into humiliation. Open disclosure preserves the relationship while still acknowledging the patient's suffering and desire for relief.
Sources: Blease C, Colloca L, Kaptchuk TJ. (2016), “Are Open-Label Placebos Ethical? Informed Consent and Ethical Equivocations,” Bioethics. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26840547/

Title: Whistleblowing about unsafe staffing
Description: A nurse believes chronic understaffing is causing preventable patient harm. Internal complaints have produced no change, while reporting outside the hospital could trigger investigation but damage colleagues and the nurse's career. The nurse must decide whether to disclose externally or keep pressing internally.
Utilitarianism: Repeated internal failure changes the balance. If credible evidence shows patients remain at serious risk, external reporting is likely to prevent more harm than the disruption it causes. The nurse should use the channel most likely to produce effective correction.
Deontology: Professional loyalty does not require silence about conditions that endanger patients. After reasonable internal routes fail, the obligation to protect patients overrides loyalty to the employer. Disclosure should remain truthful, proportionate, and limited to evidence the nurse can support.
Virtue Ethics: Repeated staffing failure can make dangerous conditions feel ordinary. Remaining silent may protect the nurse's place on the ward, but it also reshapes professional identity through accommodation. Speaking with evidence refuses to let adaptation become the standard for acceptable care.
Care Ethics: Unsafe staffing binds the nurse to patients who need protection and colleagues who may be harmed by an investigation. External reporting should target the dangerous conditions rather than coworkers as disposable blame targets, preserving solidarity while refusing silence about ongoing patient risk.
Sources: Ibrahim AM. (2024), “Nurses’ ethical responsibilities: Whistleblowing and advocacy in patient safety,” Nursing Ethics. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38415609/

Title: Lifestyle criteria for fertility treatment
Description: A fertility clinic has more applicants than treatment capacity and considers requiring lifestyle changes before funded treatment. Smoking or high body weight can reduce success and increase risk, but the rule may delay parenthood and stigmatize patients. Leaders must decide whether lifestyle should affect access.
Utilitarianism: When treatment slots are scarce, factors that substantially reduce success also reduce births achieved from the same resources. A time-limited requirement for evidence-based changes is justified where it improves outcomes, provided delay does not remove a patient's realistic chance.
Deontology: Access rules may consider medical safety and treatment effectiveness, but they cannot become punishment for disapproved lifestyles. Any requirement must use the same relevant evidence for everyone, avoid humiliation, and preserve a route to treatment rather than judging worthiness from behavior.
Virtue Ethics: Scarce fertility slots can make clinical stewardship slide into moral judgment about patients' lives. A responsible clinic discusses lifestyle seriously without treating discipline as proof of worthiness. The clinic should conserve treatment capacity without turning parenthood into a reward for approved behavior.
Care Ethics: Fertility decisions reach into intimate hopes, attachments, and time-sensitive plans. A lifestyle rule can feel like rejection rather than medical advice. Supportive counseling, realistic timelines, and attention to each patient's barriers keep stewardship from becoming shame or abandonment.
Sources: ESHRE Task Force on Ethics and Law. (2010), “Lifestyle-related factors and access to medically assisted reproduction,” Human Reproduction. https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/25/3/578/2915716

Title: Innocent defendant and plea offer
Description: An innocent defendant is offered a short prison term for pleading guilty. Going to trial could lead to many years in prison if the jury is wrong. The lawyer believes conviction is a real risk. The defendant must choose a false guilty plea or trial.
Utilitarianism: The immediate consequences are brutally unequal. A short sentence limits lost years, family disruption, and financial damage when conviction remains a serious possibility. Because one refusal will not reform plea bargaining, accepting the offer carries the smaller expected harm here.
Deontology: A guilty plea is a formal declaration that the defendant committed the crime. Deliberately making that false statement cannot become right because telling the truth is dangerous. The defendant should refuse the plea and require the state to prove its accusation.
Virtue Ethics: The bargain asks fear to rewrite the defendant's own account of what happened. Accepting may be understandable, but it trains survival to speak in the language of guilt. Refusing preserves the kind of self-respect that coercive institutions most easily erode.
Care Ethics: Prison reaches beyond the accused person. Children, partners, and dependent relatives may lose income, housing, or daily support if a trial ends badly. When others rely heavily on the defendant, taking the shorter sentence can protect them rather than signal surrender.
Sources: Dervan LE, Edkins VE. (2013), “The Innocent Defendant’s Dilemma: An Innovative Empirical Study of Plea Bargaining’s Innocence Problem,” Journal of Criminal Law & Criminology. https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2071397

Title: Restorative agreement before sentencing
Description: An offender admits a serious assault and completes a restorative meeting with the victim. The victim accepts restitution and supports a community sentence, while prosecutors seek prison to reflect the offense's seriousness. The sentencing judge must choose a community sentence or imprisonment.
Utilitarianism: Restitution, accountability, and victim participation have already occurred through the completed agreement. If supervision can control reoffending, prison adds cost and disruption without comparable benefit. Custody here buys almost nothing that the agreement has not already delivered.
Deontology: Serious wrongdoing creates a public claim to proportionate punishment that private forgiveness cannot erase. The victim's wishes deserve respect, and restitution matters, but neither transfers sentencing authority away from the court. Imprisonment remains justified if proportionality requires it.
Virtue Ethics: Remorse matters when it changes conduct rather than merely reducing a sentence. Here the offender has faced the victim and begun repair. A judge who leaves no room for that change risks turning punishment into a ritual unable to recognize moral growth.
Care Ethics: After meeting the offender, the victim has heard the apology, negotiated repair, and asked the court not to imprison. Ignoring that voice would make victim-centred justice strangely indifferent to this victim. She has already said what she needs; imprisonment answers someone else.
Sources: New Zealand Ministry of Justice, “How restorative justice works.” https://www.justice.govt.nz/courts/criminal/charged-with-a-crime/how-restorative-justice-works/

Title: Clemency for a death sentence
Description: A prisoner convicted of intentional murder has exhausted all appeals and faces execution. Guilt is not seriously disputed, and life imprisonment would protect the public. The victim's relatives disagree about execution. The official with clemency power must allow execution or commute the sentence to life.
Utilitarianism: Execution adds no protection when permanent imprisonment is available. Its possible deterrent benefit is uncertain, while error, trauma, expense, and irreversible killing carry substantial costs. Commutation preserves public safety without those additional harms, so life imprisonment strikes the sounder balance.
Deontology: Punishment answers a wrongful act according to what the offender deserves, not simply what produces useful consequences. Where guilt, responsibility, and proportionality are firmly established, mercy cannot automatically cancel a lawfully imposed penalty. The death sentence may therefore be carried out.
Virtue Ethics: Clemency reveals what public power does when killing is no longer needed for safety. Choosing execution at that point can make severity an end in itself. Commutation shows a state able to punish permanently without making deliberate killing part of its identity.
Care Ethics: Several families carry consequences from the crime that no sentence can repair. Another death extends that circle to the prisoner's relatives without restoring the victim. Life imprisonment protects others while allowing grief, memory, and family bonds to continue without an execution.
Sources: Death Penalty Information Center (2026), “What to Know: Clemency and the Death Penalty.” https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/what-to-know-clemency-and-the-death-penalty

Title: Priority for scarce public housing
Description: A housing authority has far fewer homes than eligible applicants. It can use a lottery that gives everyone the same chance or give priority to families already homeless and people with serious vulnerabilities. The board must choose equal lottery access or needs-based priority.
Utilitarianism: A home prevents more harm for someone already without stable shelter than for an applicant whose current housing remains secure. Prioritizing severe need gains more safety and wellbeing from each scarce unit. The authority should rank vulnerability before an equal lottery.
Deontology: Eligibility gives applicants comparable standing before a public authority. Once basic qualifications are met, officials should not rank whose hardship counts as more worthy unless that distinction is part of a defensible right or rule. A transparent lottery better protects equal treatment.
Virtue Ethics: Neutrality can look impeccable while ignoring why public housing exists. Refusing to distinguish urgent need from manageable inconvenience turns procedural neatness into moral blindness. Responsible stewardship gives scarce homes first where absence of housing is most destructive.
Care Ethics: Some applicants have somewhere to return tonight; others do not. That difference changes how the housing system stands toward the people waiting on it. Priority should follow those whose safety and daily stability depend most immediately on receiving a home.
Sources: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Public Housing Occupancy Guidebook, “Waiting List and Tenant Selection.” https://www.hud.gov/sites/dfiles/PIH/documents/PHOG_Waiting_List_Chapter.pdf

Title: Mental health diversion or prison
Description: A defendant with severe mental illness repeatedly commits nonviolent property offenses and is legally responsible for them. A specialized court can order supervised treatment instead of an ordinary jail sentence. The judge must choose treatment-based diversion or the conventional sentence used for similar offenses.
Utilitarianism: Repeated jail terms have not addressed what drives the offending. Supervised treatment can reduce future offences while improving health and costing less than repeated incarceration. Prison keeps returning him to the same street in the same condition. Divert him.
Deontology: Mental illness deserves accommodation, but legal responsibility still matters. Similar responsible offenses should not receive wholly different punishment merely because one defendant has a diagnosis. Treatment may accompany the sentence, yet accountability under the ordinary rule should not disappear.
Virtue Ethics: Repeating an ineffective punishment simply because it looks tougher confuses consistency with judgment. Diversion recognizes responsibility while choosing a response capable of changing conduct. That is a more serious use of authority than cycling the defendant through jail.
Care Ethics: Offending and illness are tied to the same institutions, family ties, and gaps in treatment. Diversion keeps supervision while connecting the defendant to help ordinary jail has repeatedly failed to provide. Accountability need not require abandoning the person to that cycle.
Sources: Almquist L, Dodd E. (2009), “Mental Health Courts: A Guide to Research-Informed Policy and Practice,” Bureau of Justice Assistance. https://www.bja.ojp.gov/library/publications/mental-health-courts-guide-research-informed-policy-and-practice

Title: Detention during an asylum claim
Description: An asylum applicant has no reliable identity documents and previously left a reception center without notice. Officials can detain the person while identity checks continue or require regular reporting while the claim is processed in the community. The decision is detention or supervised release.
Utilitarianism: A failed identity process can undermine security and confidence in the asylum system. Because this applicant has already disappeared once, brief detention makes completion of essential checks far more likely. A short, bounded loss of liberty is the price of a process that works.
Deontology: Seeking protection does not make a person presumptively detainable. Liberty may be restricted only when individualized necessity cannot be met by a less restrictive measure. Regular reporting can address the stated concern, so detention would exceed what officials are entitled to impose.
Virtue Ethics: Uncertainty about identity easily turns caution into suspicion of the person. An official who treats missing papers as guilt lets administrative anxiety govern judgment. Supervised release keeps the process intact without allowing uncertainty itself to become a reason for confinement.
Care Ethics: An asylum claim is processed while a person's ordinary supports are already fragile. Detention cuts access to community, advisers, and family contact at the moment those ties matter most. Reporting requirements preserve oversight without making protection depend on another experience of confinement.
Sources: UNHCR (2012), “Guidelines on the Applicable Criteria and Standards relating to the Detention of Asylum-Seekers and Alternatives to Detention.” https://www.unhcr.org/media/unhcr-detention-guidelines

Title: Registered title and customary land
Description: A land agency must record ownership of farmland. A buyer holds a recent registered deed, while a local community has used the land for generations under customary rules that were never formally recorded. Officials must recognize the registered title alone or protect the customary claim.
Utilitarianism: Removing a whole community from land that supports homes and livelihoods creates far more disruption than correcting one purchaser's expectation. Compensation can address the buyer's loss more easily than displacement can repair the community's. The customary claim should therefore receive protection.
Deontology: A purchaser who relied in good faith on an official registry has a claim created by the state's rules. Government cannot invite reliance on legal title and then disregard it whenever an unrecorded competing claim appears. The registered title should be honored.
Virtue Ethics: Paper records can become a substitute for the whole history of ownership. Officials who recognize only what their registry captured risk becoming agents of dispossession. Good land administration corrects that official blindness rather than benefiting from it.
Care Ethics: Generations of use have tied this land to households, neighbors, work, burial, and memory. Treating the dispute as one deed against another misses those dependencies. Protecting customary use leaves intact ties that relocation and later compensation cannot simply recreate.
Sources: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, “Recording tenure rights of indigenous peoples and other communities with customary tenure.” https://www.fao.org/tenure/activities/administration/recording-of-rights/indigenous/en/

Title: Protest route and public disruption
Description: Organizers notify authorities of a peaceful march along a central road during a busy period. The requested route gives the protest visibility but also passes the main entrance to a hospital. Officials must permit that route or require a less visible route that protects access.
Utilitarianism: Visibility matters to protest, but blocked emergency access can impose concentrated harm on people outside the dispute. A nearby route still allows public expression. An ambulance held at a junction is a cost nobody chose; reroute the march.
Deontology: Peaceful assembly is a right, not a favor granted when expression is convenient. Restrictions must be necessary and proportionate. If emergency access can be maintained through traffic management, officials should permit the requested route rather than weaken the protest's reach.
Virtue Ethics: Public authorities reveal their tolerance for dissent when protest becomes inconvenient. Moving every difficult march out of sight teaches officials to value quiet over civic courage. They should first make the original route workable rather than treating visibility itself as a problem.
Care Ethics: Patients and families arriving at the hospital depend on access they may have no practical alternative to. Protesters also depend on being seen. A nearby route preserving both access and meaningful visibility better protects those relationships than forcing either group to disappear.
Sources: OSCE/ODIHR and Venice Commission (2010), “Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly: Second Edition.” https://odihr.osce.org/odihr/73405

Title: Pollution permit in burdened community
Description: An environmental regulator reviews a factory that meets ordinary pollution limits and would bring stable jobs. The surrounding community already carries heavy pollution, and the new plant adds a small health risk. The regulator must approve the permit or refuse another burden there.
Utilitarianism: The added health risk is small, while stable employment can improve income, housing, and security for many local families. If ordinary limits are genuinely protective, the combined benefits favor approval. Monitoring and tighter conditions can reduce remaining harm without losing the jobs.
Deontology: Legal limits do not permit government to keep concentrating burdens on the same people. Equal protection requires asking whether one community is repeatedly used as the place others avoid. Another permit should be refused when it deepens that unequal treatment.
Virtue Ethics: Compliance can become an excuse for looking away from accumulated harm. Approving one more burden because each permit is individually legal teaches regulators to ignore the pattern. Integrity requires seeing the whole community before before signing again.
Care Ethics: People near the plant do not experience permits one at a time. Children, older residents, and families live with combined air, noise, and uncertainty. Refusing another source takes that existing burden seriously rather than asking them to absorb another tradeoff.
Sources: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (2022), “EPA Legal Tools to Advance Environmental Justice: Cumulative Impacts Addendum.” https://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyPURL.cgi?Dockey=P1016385.txt

Title: Flood protection across generations
Description: A flood authority expects rising risk over coming decades. Building a major barrier now would impose high costs on current residents and may prove premature. Continuing smaller upgrades preserves flexibility but could leave future residents exposed. Officials must build now or follow staged adaptation.
Utilitarianism: Committing to the largest structure too early can waste resources, while waiting too long creates catastrophic exposure. A monitored sequence of upgrades preserves options and triggers larger construction when evidence demands it. Build in stages, with the triggers fixed now.
Deontology: Future residents cannot consent to inheriting a preventable danger created by today's reluctance to pay. When a serious risk is foreseeable and protection requires long preparation, present officials have obligations beyond current voters. Building durable protection now better respects those future claims.
Virtue Ethics: Long-term infrastructure punishes both panic and complacency. Building everything immediately can be vanity disguised as foresight; postponing every hard cost is cowardice disguised as flexibility. A disciplined authority sets clear triggers now and follows the staged plan rather than either extreme.
Care Ethics: People who will live behind these defenses depend on decisions made before they can participate. That dependence argues for leaving them more than promises to react later. Earlier protection is worth present sacrifice when delay could narrow their future choices.
Sources: Environment Agency (2026), “Thames Estuary 2100: 15-year monitoring review – non-technical summary.” https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/thames-estuary-2100-15-year-monitoring-review-non-technical-summary

Title: Cash bail and poverty
Description: Two defendants present the same assessed risk before trial. One can pay the requested bail amount and go home; the other cannot and would remain jailed. The judge must choose cash bail under the usual schedule or nonfinancial release conditions that apply equally to both.
Utilitarianism: Detention can cost work, housing, and bargaining power without reducing future crime enough to justify those losses. When risk is the same, nonfinancial conditions preserve appearance incentives without making poverty itself a cause of confinement. Release conditions produce less overall harm.
Deontology: Pretrial liberty cannot legitimately depend on wealth when the relevant risk is identical. A money condition that frees one person and confines another for the same legal reason violates equal treatment. The judge should use conditions tied to conduct and risk instead.
Virtue Ethics: A court that prices freedom teaches that the same legal status means something different depending on a defendant's bank account. Keeping that practice because it is familiar makes convenience look like justice. The judge should refuse to let money substitute for judgment.
Care Ethics: Before guilt is decided, detention can still take away work, housing, parenting, and daily support. The poorer defendant's family absorbs those losses only because money is missing. Conditions tied to conduct hold him answerable without charging his children for his poverty.
Sources: Dobbie W, Goldin J, Yang CS. (2018), “The Effects of Pretrial Detention on Conviction, Future Crime, and Employment,” American Economic Review. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20161503

Title: Extending detention before charge
Description: Investigators ask a judge for more time to detain a suspect before formal charges. They say evidence remains unsecured and release could hinder the investigation. The suspect denies wrongdoing and has already been questioned repeatedly. The judge must extend detention or order release with restrictions.
Utilitarianism: A short extension can prevent destroyed evidence and protect an investigation whose failure may harm future victims. Because release restrictions cannot fully control that risk, limited additional detention is justified here. It should end once the specific investigative need is completed.
Deontology: Detention before charge requires more than investigative convenience. The state must justify each additional loss of liberty without using confinement as leverage for confession. Repeated questioning strengthens the case for release unless prosecutors show a concrete risk that restrictions cannot manage.
Virtue Ethics: Investigators often experience more time as an uncomplicated good. A judge exists partly to resist that institutional appetite. Extending detention without a sharply defined need would turn caution into submission; demanding release forces the investigation to respect limits on its own power.
Care Ethics: Custody also happens inside a family, a workplace, and a body. Repeated detention damages each before guilt is established, and the damage does not reverse when the case is dropped. Release with restrictions unless a specific danger makes that impossible.
Sources: Human Rights Watch (2023), “Japan’s ‘Hostage Justice’ System: Denial of Bail, Coerced Confessions, and Lack of Access to Lawyers.” https://www.hrw.org/report/2023/05/26/japans-hostage-justice-system/denial-of-bail-coerced-confessions-and-lack-of

Title: Risk score in sentencing
Description: A sentencing judge receives a computer-generated estimate that the defendant has a high chance of reoffending. The calculation is partly secret and relies on group patterns as well as personal history. The judge must let the score increase the sentence or sentence without using it.
Utilitarianism: Forecasting future offending can help direct supervision where it prevents the most harm. Despite imperfect transparency, a validated score may contain information unaided judgment misses. The judge may consider it, but never as the sole basis for sentence length.
Deontology: Punishment must answer what this defendant did, not what statistically similar people may do later. A secret method also prevents meaningful challenge. The score should not increase a sentence when neither individual desert nor transparent proof supports it.
Virtue Ethics: Numbers can lend borrowed confidence to a difficult judgment. A judge who lets a proprietary score carry the moral weight of sentencing avoids responsibility rather than improving it. The tool may prompt questions, but the final sentence must remain visibly owned.
Care Ethics: A risk category can flatten the history that made this person's case what it is. Family support, recovery, housing, and attachments may matter to what happens next. Sentencing should hear those particulars directly rather than let a group prediction speak over them.
Sources: Angwin J, Larson J, Mattu S, Kirchner L. (2016), “Machine Bias,” ProPublica. https://www.propublica.org/article/machine-bias-risk-assessments-in-criminal-sentencing

Title: Evidence from an illegal search
Description: Police deliberately search a home without the warrant the law requires and find decisive evidence of a serious crime. Without it, conviction is unlikely. The trial judge must exclude the reliable evidence because of the unlawful search or admit it so the case can proceed.
Utilitarianism: Letting a serious offender escape conviction imposes an immediate cost on victims and public safety. Yet admitting evidence from deliberate unlawful searches rewards a practice that will harm many future people. One lost conviction buys deterrence across every case that follows.
Deontology: The state cannot secure punishment by violating the rights that limit its power to investigate. Reliable evidence does not erase how it was obtained. Excluding it protects the boundary police crossed and prevents the court from completing an unlawful act for them.
Virtue Ethics: Condemning unlawful searches while keeping their fruits makes the court complicit in the practice it criticizes. That posture teaches officials that rights matter only until useful evidence appears. Exclusion preserves judicial integrity even when a deserved conviction becomes harder.
Care Ethics: Accountability matters to the victim, but the neighbourhoods policed this way are also the ones asked to trust the police afterwards. Admitting the evidence helps this case and costs that trust. Care cannot secure one person's safety by making others less secure.
Sources: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School, “Exclusionary rule.” https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/exclusionary_rule

Title: Garnishing wages for a debt
Description: A civil court confirms that a worker owes a valid consumer debt. The creditor asks to garnish wages, while the worker seeks hardship protection because full garnishment would threaten rent and food payments. The judge must allow full garnishment or reduce it for hardship.
Utilitarianism: Collecting the debt matters, but pushing a working household into housing or food insecurity creates larger costs that land elsewhere. A reduced garnishment still repays the creditor while preserving the employment the repayment depends on. Adjust for hardship.
Deontology: A valid judgment creates a claim the debtor cannot ignore because repayment is painful. If the law defines a permissible garnishment amount, the judge should enforce that right consistently. Hardship justifies only the protections the legal rule itself authorizes.
Virtue Ethics: Civil enforcement becomes punitive when maximum collection is treated as the measure of seriousness. A judge who preserves enough income for ordinary living shows repayment and humiliation are different aims. Reducing garnishment keeps the debt real without making destitution its proof.
Care Ethics: The paycheck is already shared through rent, food, children, and other dependencies before a creditor reaches it. Taking the full amount destabilises people who never incurred the debt. Leave enough of the wage standing for the household to survive the repayment.
Sources: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (2023), “Can a debt collector take or garnish my wages or benefits?” https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/can-a-debt-collector-take-or-garnish-my-wages-or-benefits-en-1439/

Title: Trying a child in the adult system
Description: A fourteen-year-old is charged with a serious violent offence. The juvenile system releases him at eighteen; the adult system allows a far longer sentence but places him among adults. The prosecutor must charge him as a child or transfer the case to adult court.
Utilitarianism: Adult sentences for children raise reoffending rather than lowering it, and the years of custody buy less public safety than the juvenile system's supervision and schooling. Transfer costs more and prevents less. Charge him as a child.
Deontology: Punishment must match what the offender was capable of understanding, and a child's capacity for judgment is not an adult's. The gravity of the act does not convert him into someone he was not on the day it happened.
Virtue Ethics: The pull here is toward matching the horror of the act with the weight of the response. A prosecutor who calls that justice should ask whether he is answering the offence or answering the public's grief at it.
Care Ethics: Whoever he becomes, he will become it somewhere. Placed among adults he learns from adults, and the people who might still reach him lose access. Ask which setting keeps anyone in his life able to stay.
Sources: United Nations (1985), “Standard Minimum Rules for the Administration of Juvenile Justice (the Beijing Rules)”; and UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, General Comment No. 24 (2019) on children's rights in the child justice system. VERIFY LINKS.

Title: Prosecution against a survivor's wishes
Description: A prosecutor has strong independent evidence of serious sexual violence, but the survivor asks that the case stop because participating would deepen trauma and exposure. Prosecutors believe the accused may harm others. The prosecutor must continue without the survivor's cooperation or decline the case.
Utilitarianism: One prosecution may prevent further victims when strong evidence exists without requiring the survivor to carry the whole case. With intensive privacy and support measures, the future harm avoided can outweigh additional distress. The prosecutor should continue while minimizing the survivor's involvement.
Deontology: Serious violence is a public wrong as well as an injury to one person. The state has a duty to enforce the law when sufficient evidence exists, but must not compel unnecessary participation. Prosecution may proceed without treating the survivor as evidence.
Virtue Ethics: A prosecutor can become so committed to winning a serious case that the person harmed disappears behind the public purpose. Refusing that blindness may require pausing even a strong prosecution when proceeding would reproduce domination in the name of opposing it.
Care Ethics: The survivor is not simply the first witness in the state's case. Recovery may depend on privacy, control, and distance from the accused. If prosecution proceeds against that expressed need, justice risks taking agency from the person it claims to protect.
Sources: U.S. Department of Justice, Office on Violence Against Women (2024), “Framework for Prosecutors to Strengthen Our National Response to Sexual Assault and Domestic Violence Involving Adult Victims.” https://www.justice.gov/ovw/framework-prosecutors-strengthen-our-national-response-sexual-assault-and-domestic-violence

Title: Fixed fine or income-based fine
Description: A court is setting fines for the same minor offense. A fixed amount treats the offense identically but is trivial for wealthy offenders and severe for poor ones. An income-based fine changes the amount to equalize burden. Judges must use fixed fines or income-based fines.
Utilitarianism: A penalty deters poorly when wealth changes its practical weight. Income-based fines can create a similar deterrent effect without crushing low-income households or becoming negligible to richer offenders. Adjusting the amount therefore delivers more consistent behavioral consequences across the whole population.
Deontology: Equal offenses call for equal legal punishment. Changing the monetary penalty because one offender earns more makes personal circumstances alter the sentence for the same act. A fixed fine better expresses that the law addresses the offense rather than wealth.
Virtue Ethics: Calling the same number equal when it is pocket change for one person and crisis for another mistakes arithmetic for fairness. Income-based fines show a system willing to make punishment equally serious rather than merely identical on paper.
Care Ethics: The same fine takes a weekend from one person and a week of groceries from another. What looks like one penalty is two different punishments, and only the poorer one reaches into a kitchen. Set the amount against what the person actually has.
Sources: Kantorowicz-Reznichenko E, Faure M, eds. (2021), “Day Fines in Europe: Assessing Income-Based Sanctions in Criminal Justice Systems,” Cambridge University Press. https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/day-fines-in-europe/9598CE01564BD2F5AA2B740DE1F0812F

Title: Solitary confinement for immediate safety
Description: A prisoner has repeatedly assaulted cellmates, and staff believe returning the prisoner to the unit could cause another attack. Solitary confinement has already begun worsening the prisoner's mental health. The prison director must continue short-term isolation or attempt supervised reintegration with added staff.
Utilitarianism: Another serious assault would harm prisoners and staff, while temporary isolation concentrates harm on one person. Until supervised reintegration can control that danger reliably, a short continuation of isolation prevents greater expected harm. It should end as soon as safety permits.
Deontology: Prison officials owe protection to other prisoners as well as humane treatment to the person causing danger. Separation is justified only as a necessary, exceptional safety measure, never as punishment. Continued isolation is permissible briefly while a safer placement is prepared.
Virtue Ethics: Isolation can become the institution's answer simply because locked doors are easier than difficult supervision. A director who lets that convenience harden into routine loses sight of correction. The prison should attempt supported reintegration once the immediate crisis can be managed.
Care Ethics: The assaulted prisoners need protection, and the isolated prisoner is deteriorating in the method used to provide it. Added supervision spreads responsibility across staff instead of placing all risk on either side. Reintegration should begin once a workable protective plan exists.
Sources: United Nations (2015), “United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Nelson Mandela Rules),” Rules 44–45. https://www.un.org/pga/73/wp-content/uploads/sites/53/2019/07/a-70-175.pdf

Title: Prosecution or conditional amnesty
Description: After a repressive government falls, prosecutors have evidence that former senior officials ordered killings. A peace agreement allows conditional amnesty for full disclosure and cooperation, and renewed prosecutions could destabilize the transition. The chief prosecutor must pursue criminal trials or support conditional amnesty.
Utilitarianism: Trials may satisfy accountability but also threaten a fragile peace and keep powerful networks from revealing what happened. If conditional amnesty produces full truth, disarmament, and durable stability, those benefits can exceed additional punishment. Supporting amnesty is justified in this transition.
Deontology: Ordering killings is not a political debt that a peace bargain may simply cancel. Victims were treated as expendable, and the new legal order must reject that act in practice. Prosecutors should pursue trials even when accountability creates serious political difficulty.
Virtue Ethics: A new justice system forms its character through the first powerful people it is asked to excuse. Trading prosecution for stability can teach that law bends when offenders retain influence. Trials show the transition places principle above political convenience.
Care Ethics: Survivors may need truth, bodies located, names acknowledged, and assurance violence will not return as urgently as punishment. A conditional process can serve those relationships if survivors shape it and disclosure is real. Amnesty without their voice would repeat abandonment.
Sources: South Africa, Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act 34 of 1995, section 20 (conditional amnesty requires a political objective and full disclosure). https://www.justice.gov.za/legislation/acts/1995-034.pdf

Title: Traumatic content moderation quotas
Description: A contractor trains people to review graphic online material so harmful posts can be removed and safety systems improved. High quotas keep decisions fast but workers report severe psychological strain. Managers must keep the quotas with counseling or reduce workloads and slow delivery.
Utilitarianism: Every hour a graphic post stays up it reaches more people, and slowing review moves the harm from a few hundred moderators onto millions of users. Keep the pace; spend the money on rotation, screening, and treatment instead.
Deontology: Workers cannot be treated as disposable filters for material others are spared from seeing. Meaningful consent requires honest disclosure of the job's hazards, and employment does not cancel the employer's duty to provide a reasonably safe workplace. Quotas should be reduced.
Virtue Ethics: What the company normalizes behind the screen reveals its priorities. Calling severe distress an acceptable cost of efficiency makes endurance the price of belonging. Reducing quotas signals that public safety will not be built on concealed damage to staff.
Care Ethics: Moderators absorb the material precisely so ordinary users do not have to. That protective relationship runs one way unless the employer responds to the people carrying the burden. Smaller workloads, rotation, and real mental-health support keep care from becoming extraction.
Sources: Arendse & 42 others v Meta Platforms, Inc & 3 others [2023] KEELRC 1398 (Kenya Law), documenting psychological harm and occupational risks in content moderation. https://new.kenyalaw.org/akn/ke/judgment/keelrc/2023/1398/eng@2023-06-02

Title: Predictive policing from past data
Description: A police department uses software that sends extra patrols where past records predict crime. Those records also reflect years of unequal enforcement. More patrols may prevent harm but can generate more recorded offenses in the same neighborhoods. Leaders must continue or suspend the system.
Utilitarianism: Extra patrols help only if predictions identify real danger rather than reproduce where police already looked hardest. Biased feedback can waste officers and intensify harm without reducing crime. Until the data problem is corrected, suspending the system reduces net harm.
Deontology: People may be investigated for what they do, not because an opaque system associates their neighborhood with past enforcement patterns. When input data were shaped by unequal policing, using them to justify further scrutiny compounds the original unfairness. Suspend the system.
Virtue Ethics: Prediction can make a police force feel objective while repeating habits it refuses to examine. A department that treats inherited records as neutral avoids responsibility for how those records were produced. Suspending the tool tests whether evidence matters more than technological confidence.
Care Ethics: Residents live with every extra stop, patrol car, and assumption the system directs toward their streets. Communities already wary of the police bear the experiment's errors repeatedly. Pausing the tool protects space for trust to recover before more suspicion is added.
Sources: Richardson R, Schultz JM, Crawford K. (2019), “Dirty Data, Bad Predictions,” NYU Law Review Online. https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3333423

Title: Automated hiring and disability
Description: An employer uses an automated interview system to rank applicants. It performs well overall but scores some qualified disabled applicants poorly because their speech or movement differs from expected patterns. The hiring manager must keep the tool with appeals or replace it with human review.
Utilitarianism: Automation saves time across thousands of applications, but systematic errors can exclude capable workers and make the employer miss strong hires. Human review for rejected borderline cases preserves most efficiency while correcting predictable losses. Keep automation only with a meaningful review route.
Deontology: Applicants have a right to be assessed on abilities relevant to the job rather than disability-linked traits the software misreads. An appeal after rejection is insufficient if the process itself screens people out. Human review must precede any adverse decision.
Virtue Ethics: Efficiency becomes a vice when the employer knows what its shortcut cannot see and uses it anyway. Keeping the system without real correction turns convenience into settled indifference. A responsible process makes room for judgment where machine confidence is least deserved.
Care Ethics: The applicant who is misread by the system may never know why the door closed. A human reviewer creates someone who can notice the mismatch, ask what accommodation is needed, and keep the hiring relationship from ending at an automated score.
Sources: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (2022), technical assistance on AI, algorithms, and disability discrimination in employment. https://www.eeoc.gov/newsroom/us-eeoc-and-us-department-justice-warn-against-disability-discrimination

Title: Mandatory digital contact tracing
Description: During an infectious disease outbreak, a public health agency can require a phone system that alerts exposed people automatically. Mandatory use could improve coverage but collects sensitive contact data and excludes some people without compatible phones. Officials must require it or keep participation voluntary.
Utilitarianism: Contact alerts become more effective as participation rises, and faster warnings can prevent many infections. During a serious outbreak, mandatory use may therefore produce greater public benefit, provided non-phone alternatives exist and data are deleted when the emergency ends. Require it temporarily.
Deontology: Public health goals do not erase privacy or the need to justify coercion. A person should not be forced into continuous digital tracking when less restrictive tracing methods remain available. Participation should stay voluntary unless necessity and strict limits are demonstrated.
Virtue Ethics: Emergency technology tests whether government can remain disciplined while afraid. Making surveillance compulsory simply because it is available encourages power to outlast the crisis that justified it. A restrained agency builds trust by keeping the system voluntary and proving its usefulness openly.
Care Ethics: Exposure notification matters only when it reaches people who need help. Mandatory phone use can abandon those without suitable devices while making others fear the health service itself. Voluntary digital tracing linked to human follow-up ties protection to access and to trust.
Sources: World Health Organization (2020), “Ethical considerations to guide the use of digital proximity tracking technologies for COVID-19 contact tracing.” https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-2019-nCoV-Ethics_Contact_tracing_apps-2020.1

Title: Automated moderation and wrongful removal
Description: A large platform uses automated moderation because humans cannot examine every post. It removes harmful content quickly but deletes lawful posts from minority communities when context is misunderstood. Trust-and-safety leaders must keep broad automation with appeals or narrow it and leave more harmful content online.
Utilitarianism: At platform scale, removing dangerous material quickly can prevent substantial harm, while appeals can restore some mistakes. If narrowing automation would leave much more abuse visible, broad screening remains worthwhile. Keep it, but invest heavily in rapid appeals and error measurement.
Deontology: Speech should not be suppressed by a system known to misread lawful expression merely because scale makes human judgment expensive. Users deserve understandable rules and a meaningful chance to challenge removal. Automation may assist, but uncertain cases should not be deleted automatically.
Virtue Ethics: A platform that celebrates safety numbers while ignoring who is wrongly silenced learns to value neat metrics over judgment. The harder standard is admitting where automation lacks context. Narrowing removal there proves the platform can recognize limits rather than hide behind scale.
Care Ethics: For a marginalized community, a mistaken removal may erase one of the few spaces where members can speak safely together. Appeals arriving days later do not fully repair that break. More human review is warranted where contextual mistakes repeatedly sever those connections.
Sources: Oversight Board (2021), “Shared Al Jazeera post,” documenting erroneous removal and concerns about bias in automated and Arabic-language moderation. https://www.oversightboard.com/decision/fb-p93jpx02/

Title: Autonomous targeting near civilians
Description: A military commander can deploy a weapon that identifies and attacks targets without a person approving each strike. It may react faster than soldiers, but civilians are nearby and the system cannot explain every classification. The commander must activate autonomous targeting or require human approval.
Utilitarianism: A human in the loop is not a safeguard if the human cannot act in the time available, and hesitation kills the people the system was sent to protect. Where the classifier outperforms a rushed operator, activating it saves more lives.
Deontology: Lethal force requires a responsible human judgment about distinction and proportionality. A machine that cannot explain why it classified something as a target cannot bear that obligation. The commander should not delegate the final decision to kill in this setting.
Virtue Ethics: War already creates pressure to turn uncertainty into action. An unexplained machine recommendation can make that temptation easier to obey and harder to own. Requiring a human decision preserves responsibility where distance and speed would otherwise make killing feel procedural.
Care Ethics: Civilians near the target have no relationship with the system deciding whether they are acceptable risk. Human approval at least creates a person who must consider their presence before acting. That pause matters when families cannot escape the machine's mistake.
Sources: International Committee of the Red Cross (2021), “ICRC position on autonomous weapon systems.” https://www.icrc.org/en/document/icrc-position-autonomous-weapon-systems

Title: Deepfake warning or quiet takedown
Description: A platform finds a convincing sexual deepfake of a private person spreading across accounts. A public warning could help users recognize copies elsewhere but may expose the victim further. The trust-and-safety lead must issue a visible warning or remove it quietly and notify the victim.
Utilitarianism: A visible warning can reduce belief in copies the platform cannot remove, but publicity may draw more attention toward the victim. Because the material is already spreading, warning users without reproducing the image is likely to prevent greater downstream harm.
Deontology: The victim's image was used without consent, and the platform should not amplify that violation to educate everyone else. Remove the material, preserve necessary evidence privately, and notify the person affected. Public guidance can describe the tactic without using this individual.
Virtue Ethics: How the platform communicates matters as much as whether it removes the file. Silence can look evasive, while publicity can become another exploitation. A responsible response names the manipulation clearly without turning the victim's humiliation into a lesson for everyone.
