Care Ethics: Once the person's image is circulating, control over how others see them is already shrinking. Every public reference can widen that loss. Contacting the victim first and removing copies quietly holds the response to restoring agency rather than managing others.
Sources: Chesney R, Citron DK. (2019), “Deep Fakes: A Looming Challenge for Privacy, Democracy, and National Security,” California Law Review. https://scholarship.law.bu.edu/faculty_scholarship/640/

Title: Credit scores from mobile data
Description: A digital lender can score applicants using mobile-money and phone histories when credit records are missing. This may extend loans to people banks overlook, but the data reveal private behavior and may penalize patterns linked to poverty. Managers must use the score or require records.
Utilitarianism: Conventional records exclude many people before repayment ability is considered. Alternative data can open useful credit to borrowers who otherwise have none, and that access may outweigh privacy costs if defaults remain manageable. Use the score with auditing and data limits.
Deontology: Access to credit does not authorize a lender to treat unrelated private behavior as evidence of worthiness. Applicants should know what information determines the decision and be judged by relevant, challengeable criteria. Use conventional records or explicitly consented financial data.
Virtue Ethics: Calling the model inclusive while turning every phone action into financial evidence changes what lending means. Credit stops evaluating repayment and starts watching a person's life. Genuine inclusion requires restraint about what the lender is willing to know.
Care Ethics: People without formal credit histories often depend on the mobile accounts being mined because other financial doors are closed. Using that history can create access, but only if borrowers can understand errors and reach a human before an invisible pattern blocks them.
Sources: Johnen C, Parlasca M, Mußhoff O. (2021), “Promises and pitfalls of digital credit: Empirical evidence from Kenya,” PLOS ONE. https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0255215

Title: Emotion recognition at work
Description: An employer tests software that infers workers' emotions from faces and voices, then flags people for coaching. Managers say it may reveal stress, but the system can misread expression and turns private feelings into performance data. Leaders must use it or rely on ordinary supervision.
Utilitarianism: Catching serious stress early could help some workers, but routine emotional scoring creates false alarms, anxiety, and distorted management across the whole workforce. Ordinary supervision can identify problems without those broad harms. The employer should not deploy emotion recognition for performance decisions.
Deontology: A worker agrees to perform a job, not to have inner feelings continuously inferred and judged. Emotional states are neither reliable conduct nor property of the employer. Performance decisions should rest on observable work and direct communication rather than involuntary psychological surveillance.
Virtue Ethics: An employer that measures every expression teaches managers to distrust conversation and workers to perform the face the system rewards. That workplace becomes less candid precisely because it claims to measure honesty. Refusing the tool protects the possibility of genuine human judgment.
Care Ethics: Stress is something a supervisor should learn through relationship, not extract from a face. A worker who is struggling needs someone able to ask, listen, and respond to context. Emotion scoring can replace that connection with suspicion before any conversation begins.
Sources: European Union (2024), Artificial Intelligence Act, Article 5(1)(f), prohibiting AI emotion inference in workplaces except for medical or safety reasons. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689

Title: Digital identity and benefit access
Description: A benefits agency uses digital identity checks to prevent duplicate claims. Manual exceptions are increasingly exploited for fraud, but some eligible people repeatedly fail biometric verification. Officials must end manual exceptions and require digital verification or keep an alternative route for failed checks.
Utilitarianism: Fraud drains money from every legitimate claimant, yet excluding genuine recipients can remove food, medicine, or rent entirely. Because authentication failures affect real eligible people, a controlled manual route causes less serious harm than a digital-only rule. Keep exceptions with stronger checks.
Deontology: Eligibility for a public benefit does not disappear because a person's body or device fails authentication. The agency may investigate identity carefully, but it must provide another way to prove a valid claim. Digital verification cannot become a condition of entitlement.
Virtue Ethics: A fraud-control system becomes unjust when officials know it rejects genuine people and call that collateral error. Keeping an exception process shows the agency can protect public money without pretending technological consistency is the same thing as administrative fairness.
Care Ethics: The person locked out may already depend on the payment for ordinary survival and have no easy way to fix the technology. A staffed exception route leaves someone reachable when the system says no, preserving public support for those relying on it.
Sources: World Bank ID4D, “Biometric data – Challenges for accuracy and inclusion,” documenting authentication failures and the need for exception handling. https://id4d.worldbank.org/guide/biometric-data

Title: Teen app limits by default
Description: A social media service knows some teenagers spend long periods on its feed. A hard default time limit could reduce compulsive use but also restrict teenagers who use it for friends, hobbies, or support. Product leaders must impose the default limit or leave controls optional.
Utilitarianism: A default limit affects every teenager, including many whose use is healthy, but it also changes behavior without requiring self-control from those most vulnerable to compulsive design. The likely population benefit supports a default limit that users and families can deliberately adjust.
Deontology: Teenagers are developing autonomy, and families differ in what limits are appropriate. The platform should not silently decide how much lawful social interaction every user may have. Provide clear tools and safe defaults, but let users and guardians choose the actual limit.
Virtue Ethics: Design can either help young users practice self-command or make endless attention the business model. A default pause changes what the company encourages without banning the service. It signals that success is not measured by keeping a teenager scrolling indefinitely.
Care Ethics: For some teenagers, the feed is where friendships and support remain available after school. Cutting access automatically can isolate the very users a safety policy aims to protect. Limits should be adjustable around the relationships each young person actually depends on.
Sources: U.S. Surgeon General (2023), “Social Media and Youth Mental Health: The U.S. Surgeon General’s Advisory.” https://www.hhs.gov/surgeongeneral/reports-and-publications/youth-mental-health/social-media/index.html

Title: Data centre in a water-stressed district
Description: A company wants to build a data centre in a district with a strained water supply and few jobs. It will bring tax revenue and lasting work for a few dozen people, and draw heavily on local water. The council must approve it or refuse.
Utilitarianism: Weigh the water against everything the revenue buys: clinics, roads, and jobs in a district that has few. Water use can be capped and priced; a poor district cannot easily be made less poor. Approve it, with hard limits on draw.
Deontology: Residents did not consent to having their water allocated to a private facility, and a benefit paid to the council is not consent given by them. If the supply is already strained, the prior claim belongs to the households drawing on it.
Virtue Ethics: A council short of money finds reasons easily. The question is whether it is weighing the offer or being flattered by it, and whether anyone is willing to say aloud what the district will look like in a dry year.
Care Ethics: The jobs go to a few dozen households; the water shortage reaches every kitchen, every clinic, and every field. Ask who carries the dry season, and whether the people who will carry it were in the room when this was discussed.
Sources: Mytton D (2021), “Data centre water consumption,” npj Clean Water; and Li P et al. (2023), “Making AI Less Thirsty: Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models,” arXiv. VERIFY LINKS.

Title: Personalized prices for customers
Description: An online retailer can use browsing and purchase data to estimate what each customer will pay. Personalized prices may offer discounts to price-sensitive shoppers but charge others more for the same item without their knowledge. Executives must use individualized pricing or keep one visible price.
Utilitarianism: Different prices can expand sales to customers who would otherwise be priced out while capturing more revenue from those willing to pay. If the discounts genuinely increase access, personalized pricing can raise total welfare. Use it, but disclose that prices may vary.
Deontology: Customers buying the same product should not be secretly charged according to what hidden profiling says they can be made to tolerate. Consent and fair dealing require understandable pricing rules. A common posted price avoids manipulating information customers cannot inspect or challenge.
Virtue Ethics: Studying each customer's weakness simply to extract the highest possible amount turns knowledge into leverage. Even when legal, that trains the business to see loyalty and urgency as opportunities for exploitation. One visible price sets a better commercial character.
Care Ethics: A higher individualized price may fall on someone shopping under urgency, limited mobility, or fewer alternatives. The system cannot know what dependence sits behind willingness to pay. A common price avoids converting a customer's constrained situation into a reason to charge more.
Sources: OECD (2018), “Personalised Pricing in the Digital Era.” https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/personalised-pricing-in-the-digital-era_db4d9c9c-en.html

Title: Automating routine local news
Description: A local newsroom is losing revenue and cannot maintain its reporting staff. It can automate routine stories from public records and keep broader coverage, or retain human reporters but publish fewer local stories. Editors must choose automated volume or fewer fully reported stories.
Utilitarianism: Residents lose information when shrinking budgets erase routine coverage. Automation can preserve weather, sports, meeting, and public-record updates while reporters focus on work requiring judgment. Using it for routine stories keeps more useful local information available without abandoning human reporting.
Deontology: Readers are entitled to know who or what produced a news report and who is accountable for errors. Automation may assist, but publishing machine-written stories without meaningful editorial responsibility fails that obligation. Fewer human-reviewed stories are preferable to unaccountable volume.
Virtue Ethics: A newsroom becomes different when filling space matters more than knowing the place it covers. Automating routine material need not destroy journalism, but replacing reporters merely to preserve output count would. The newsroom should protect human reporting even if publication volume falls.
Care Ethics: Local reporting depends on trust with residents who call, explain, correct, and trust particular journalists over time. Automated stories can preserve facts but not those connections. Fewer human-written stories may serve the community better where relationships are how important stories surface.
Sources: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism (2024), “Journalism, media, and technology trends and predictions 2024.” https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/journalism-media-and-technology-trends-and-predictions-2024

Title: Deleting face data after exit
Description: A photo service lets a user delete an account. The company can remove the person's photos but keep a face template learned from them because it improves recognition. The privacy lead must delete the derived face data too or retain it after account closure.
Utilitarianism: Keeping learned face templates may improve recognition for millions of users while exposing former users to a smaller continuing privacy risk. If the template cannot be used to reconstruct or identify them outside the service, retaining it could create greater net benefit.
Deontology: Deleting an account withdraws the basis on which the company received the person's biometric information. A derived face template still comes from that person and remains sensitive. The company should delete it rather than redefine withdrawal so only visible photos disappear.
Virtue Ethics: Promises of deletion mean little if the company keeps the most useful residue after a user leaves. Retaining it trains the organization to interpret every commitment in its own favor. Deleting the template makes trust costly enough to be meaningful.
Care Ethics: Leaving the service is often the only practical way a user can end the relationship. Keeping biometric traces after that exit denies closure and leaves the former user dependent on a company they deliberately left. Deletion should include what was derived.
Sources: U.S. Federal Trade Commission (2021), settlement over retention of photos, face embeddings, and facial-recognition models after account deactivation. https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2021/01/california-company-settles-ftc-allegations-it-deceived-consumers-about-use-facial-recognition-photo

Title: Safety filter blocks safe requests
Description: An AI assistant refuses many harmless questions whenever they contain words associated with dangerous topics. Loosening the filter would make the service more useful but could also let some harmful requests through. The safety team must lower the refusal threshold or keep the stricter setting.
Utilitarianism: A system that refuses harmless requests at high rates imposes costs on legitimate users, while a modestly looser threshold need not remove safety controls. If testing shows only a small rise in harmful outputs, lowering the threshold creates more benefit overall.
Deontology: Inconvenience is not a wrong done to the user; a person refused an answer can look elsewhere. Someone harmed by an answer the service supplied cannot undo it. The provider owes more to the second person than the first.
Virtue Ethics: Exaggerated refusal can look responsible because nothing dangerous gets through, but complete caution is not judgment. A capable system must learn when risk is real and when fear is merely lexical. Loosening the filter after testing reflects confidence disciplined by evidence.
Care Ethics: A harmless user repeatedly refused by the system is left without explanation or help, especially when the topic is difficult to discuss. Better responses can preserve boundaries while staying present. Reduce blanket refusals and offer safer guidance where possible.
Sources: Röttger P et al. (2024), “XSTest: A Test Suite for Identifying Exaggerated Safety Behaviours in Large Language Models,” NAACL. https://aclanthology.org/2024.naacl-long.301/

Title: AI companion and human contact
Description: A care service offers conversational AI to older adults who report loneliness. Some users say it provides comfort, but a few begin calling relatives less often. Program managers must expand unrestricted access or limit daily use and pair the tool with human contact.
Utilitarianism: Companionship that reliably reduces loneliness is a real benefit, but replacing human contact can worsen isolation over time. Limited use linked to calls, visits, or group activities keeps the immediate comfort while protecting broader social connection. Pair the tool with human contact.
Deontology: Users may choose artificial companionship if they understand what the system is and how it works. The service should not manipulate attachment or present the machine as a human relationship. Access can continue, but only with clear disclosure and meaningful user control.
Virtue Ethics: Simulated companionship can satisfy a care program because it is easier to scale than human presence. That makes efficiency look like friendship. Limiting the tool keeps technology in a supporting role rather than letting convenience redefine what companionship means.
Care Ethics: For someone whose children rarely call, the machine is not competing with a relationship; it is what there is at four in the morning. Taking it away to encourage contact that may not come serves the programme's ideal, not the person.
Sources: New York State Office for the Aging (2023), “NYSOFA’s Rollout of AI Companion Robot ElliQ Shows 95% Reduction in Loneliness,” documenting a public program providing AI companions to older adults. https://apps.cio.ny.gov/apps/mediacontact/public/view.cfm?parm=E4E6D5FF-C4A8-BF7F-60D8C2CB69442AF4

Title: Moderation in a low-resource language
Description: A platform has few trained reviewers for a language used by millions. An automated system can remove more dangerous posts quickly, but it often misses local context and wrongly deletes lawful speech. Leaders must deploy it broadly now or wait for better language-specific moderation.
Utilitarianism: Leaving violent or hateful material online can cause serious harm at scale, and waiting for perfect language support may take years. Broad automation should be deployed now, but paired with fast local appeals and continuous retraining to reduce predictable contextual errors.
Deontology: Users should not receive weaker speech protections because their language is less profitable to support. A system known to misunderstand context cannot be given broad power to silence them. The platform should build competent language review before relying on automatic removal.
Virtue Ethics: Global reach creates obligations that cannot be met by translating an English solution halfway. Deploying a weak system and calling coverage complete would reveal indifference disguised as speed. The platform should invest in the linguistic knowledge its own expansion made necessary.
Care Ethics: Language carries jokes, insults, grief, political memory, and danger through ties outsiders may not see. Moderation without people who understand those connections can harm the same communities it aims to protect. Local reviewers should shape the system before broad enforcement.
Sources: Oversight Board (2022), “Reclaiming Arabic words,” documenting moderation errors and recommending language-specific guidance and resources. https://www.oversightboard.com/decision/ig-2pj00l4t/

Title: Facial recognition at school entrances
Description: A school uses facial recognition at entrances to speed attendance and identify people who should not enter. It reduces checks but stores children's biometric data and is less accurate for some groups. School leaders must keep facial recognition or return to cards and staff checks.
Utilitarianism: Faster entry and security gains are useful, but ordinary cards and staff checks already provide workable alternatives without biometric error or lifelong data exposure. Because the added benefit is modest, returning to less intrusive methods prevents more harm than it forgoes.
Deontology: Children should not have to surrender biometric identifiers simply to enter school when less intrusive identification works. Their faces are not ordinary credentials that can be replaced after a breach. Attendance and security should use methods that respect bodily privacy.
Virtue Ethics: Daily face scanning teaches students what kind of institution they are entering. A school that makes surveillance routine for convenience risks confusing control with safety. Returning to ordinary checks shows technology is adopted for necessity, not simply because it can be installed.
Care Ethics: School entry is part of a child's everyday life with teachers and classmates. Turning that moment into a biometric checkpoint can make some families feel watched before learning begins. Human checks preserve room for recognition to remain personal rather than purely technical.
Sources: Galligan C, Rosenfeld H, Kleinman M, Parthasarathy S. (2020), “Cameras in the Classroom: Facial Recognition Technology in Schools,” University of Michigan. https://stpp.fordschool.umich.edu/research/research-report/cameras-classroom-facial-recognition-technology-schools

Title: Open release of cyber AI
Description: A research lab develops an AI system that finds software weaknesses and generates attack code. Open release could help defenders secure systems quickly, but attackers could use the same capability immediately. Leaders must publish it openly or restrict access to vetted security users.
Utilitarianism: Defenders gain from broad access, but attackers need only one successful exploit to cause widespread damage before patches exist. Restricting access to vetted users preserves substantial defensive value while reducing immediate misuse. The lab should not release the full capability openly.
Deontology: People running vulnerable systems are entitled to know what is wrong with them, and a lab that withholds that knowledge decides on their behalf that they cannot be trusted with it. Publish, and let defenders act on their own systems.
Virtue Ethics: Openness is valuable, but treating publication as automatically courageous can become a way to escape responsibility for consequences. A mature research culture knows when restraint is part of scientific seriousness. Controlled access keeps the lab answerable for what its work enables.
Care Ethics: People exposed by a new exploit are usually absent from the release decision and may not know their systems are vulnerable. Restricting access keeps developers closer to those downstream risks while giving defenders time to repair before offensive capability spreads.
Sources: NIST (2024), “Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models,” SP 800-218A. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/a/final

Title: Grouping pupils by attainment
Description: A secondary school is deciding how to organize classes. Grouping pupils by current attainment may help teachers target lessons, but lower groups can face weaker expectations. Mixed classes avoid fixed labels but are harder to teach. The school must choose attainment groups or mixed classes.
Utilitarianism: Teaching aimed at a narrower range reaches more pupils effectively than teaching pitched at everyone at once. Where movement between groups stays genuinely open, grouping raises total attainment enough to outweigh the misplacement it causes. On balance, group them.
Deontology: Early grouping changes what a school offers. Lower placement cannot become a ceiling on what a pupil is taught. Any grouping system must use fair criteria and give every pupil a genuine, practical route into more demanding work.
Virtue Ethics: Lower sets can harden into ordinary expectations. Teachers may begin expecting less from lower sets and call it realism. A school that normalizes that drift stops educating ambition and starts reproducing its own early judgments.
Care Ethics: Placement also rearranges everyday classroom connections. A pupil placed low may lose adults who knew their progress and enter a room already treated as weaker. Mixed classes better preserve continuity and the chance to be noticed as learning changes.
Sources: Education Endowment Foundation, “Setting and streaming.” https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/teaching-learning-toolkit/setting-and-streaming

Title: Make-up exams after illness
Description: A secondary school is revising its exam policy. Allowing make-up tests after documented illness protects students from chance setbacks but adds work and extra preparation time. One fixed sitting is simpler and uniform. The choice is whether excused absences receive a make-up exam.
Utilitarianism: One missed sitting can distort a record. An unavoidable illness should not erase months of learning when a controlled make-up creates little extra burden. Offering one documented make-up date therefore produces a fairer result with limited system-wide cost.
Deontology: A student kept from the hall by illness has not chosen to miss the assessment, and should not carry a penalty for it. One common make-up date, documented cause, and identical standards keep treatment equal without pretending every absence is the same.
Virtue Ethics: Exceptions test what examination rules are for. Refusing every exception can make consistency look like rigor when it is really inflexibility. A limited make-up policy lets the school keep standards firm without turning procedural neatness into its highest value.
Care Ethics: Illness breaks the normal rhythm of assessment. A make-up exam leaves the student's place in the learning process intact while avoiding an open-ended exception. The school preserves continuity without asking classmates or teachers to absorb unlimited special arrangements.
Sources: CGS Dhaka, “Rules and Regulations” — school policy documents no make-up tests and use of alternative assessment. https://www.cgsd.edu.bd/copy-of-uniform

Title: Funding allocation between schools
Description: An education authority has extra funding that cannot meet every school's needs. Equal shares are simple and visible. Giving more to schools serving poorer pupils may address deeper barriers but leaves others with less. Officials must choose equal increases or needs-based funding.
Utilitarianism: The same grant has different effects. A classroom lacking books or support can improve more from the same grant than one already well supplied. Directing more funds toward disadvantaged schools therefore creates the greater total educational benefit.
Deontology: Pupils are owed a genuine opportunity to learn, not an identical envelope. Where basic provision is already weaker, more may be directed there without wronging anyone, provided the basis for allocation stays public, consistent, and free of political influence.
Virtue Ethics: An equal split can hide unequal conditions. Spreading money evenly can look fair while avoiding harder judgments about need. A responsible authority accepts the discomfort of unequal grants when equal shares would preserve unequal schooling.
Care Ethics: Public schools carry very different levels of dependence. Where families have few alternatives, missing resources are harder to replace. Needs-based funding draws the system closer to those communities while preserving trust through clear explanations to schools receiving smaller increases.
Sources: South African Government (2024), “South African Schools Act: National Norms and Standards for School Funding.” https://www.gov.za/documents/notices/south-african-schools-act-national-norms-and-standards-school-funding-30-sep-2024

Title: Language used for instruction
Description: A school system must choose the main teaching language in early grades. A home language improves immediate understanding and family connection. A wider language may help later study and employment. Leaders must decide whether to begin in the home language or shift earlier.
Utilitarianism: Comprehension in the early years matters, but the wider language governs access to secondary study, employment, and information for decades afterward. Where teachers can support the transition properly, shifting earlier compounds advantage across an entire cohort's working life.
Deontology: Instruction begins with access to meaning. Children cannot receive education meaningfully in words they do not understand. A language policy may prepare pupils for wider communication, but administrative convenience cannot justify sacrificing comprehension during the early years.
Virtue Ethics: Language policy teaches more than vocabulary. A system that abandons a child's first language too quickly treats advancement as separation from home. Good judgment instead builds confidence in both languages, preparing pupils for wider communication without making one identity a barrier.
Care Ethics: A familiar language keeps early schooling connected. It links the child, family, and teacher while unfamiliar routines are forming. Introducing a wider language gradually preserves that connection instead of making school feel foreign before trust and confidence have developed.
Sources: Jessica Ball (2011), UNESCO, “Enhancing learning of children from diverse language backgrounds: mother tongue-based bilingual or multilingual education in the early years.” https://unesdoc.unesco.org/in/documentViewer.xhtml?ark=/ark:/48223/pf0000212270

Title: Mainstream or specialist placement
Description: A placement team must decide where a disabled pupil will study. Mainstream classes offer daily learning with peers and fuller participation. A specialist setting may provide more intensive support than the local school can manage. The choice is mainstream placement with support or specialist placement.
Utilitarianism: Separate settings trade participation for concentrated support. Mainstream placement usually adds social and educational gains that separation cannot replace. Unless specialist provision is needed for substantial progress or safety, supported mainstream schooling is likely to produce the better overall outcome.
Deontology: Placement decisions shape access as well as location. The pupil has a claim to equal participation and to support that makes access meaningful. A specialist placement becomes permissible when it answers the pupil's actual needs rather than the institution's convenience.
Virtue Ethics: Inclusion can become either real or symbolic. Sending every child to a separate setting is equally revealing. The better institution is one that knows its limits, strengthens ordinary participation where possible, and admits when specialist help is necessary.
Care Ethics: School placement reorganizes a child's daily circle. Mainstream placement keeps ordinary friendships close, but only if help is dependable. The setting should be the one where familiar connections and necessary assistance can both remain real.
Sources: Finnish National Agency for Education, “Support to learning and pupil welfare system.” https://www.oph.fi/en/education-and-qualifications/support-learning-and-pupil-welfare-system

Title: Admissions preference for disadvantage
Description: A university compares two applicants with similar potential but unequal school opportunities. One has slightly higher grades from a well-resourced school; the other achieved less with serious disadvantages. The admissions committee must choose between one academic threshold and a policy that considers educational context.
Utilitarianism: Context changes what the same grade predicts. Giving some weight to educational context can identify capable students otherwise missed and widen social returns from higher education. On these facts, contextual admission is the better policy for both institutions and applicants.
Deontology: An applicant is owed judgment on what they themselves have demonstrated, not on inferences drawn from the school or household they came from. Adjusting a threshold by circumstance judges people partly by their category. Hold the threshold.
Virtue Ethics: Numbers can simplify a judgment too quickly. Treating grades as complete measures can mistake inherited opportunity for merit, while treating hardship as an automatic credential creates another shortcut. Contextual review asks selectors to exercise judgment without romanticizing either advantage or disadvantage.
Care Ethics: Educational disadvantage travels with an applicant. Family resources, school support, and earlier opportunities shape the path to the admissions table. Contextual review makes those dependencies visible, while support after admission prevents an opened door from becoming an unsupported transition.
Sources: UCAS, “Contextual admissions.” https://www.ucas.com/applying/applying-university/individual-needs/contextual-admissions

Title: Repeating or advancing a grade
Description: A school team must decide whether a struggling pupil moves to the next grade. Repeating may give more time to learn but can damage motivation and peer ties. Advancing preserves friendships but leaves gaps. The team must choose repetition or advancement with support.
Utilitarianism: Repeating a year changes more than timing. Evidence links repetition with stigma, disengagement, and later dropout, while learning gains are uncertain. Those harms usually outweigh another year of instruction, so advancement with targeted support is more likely to improve long-term outcomes.
Deontology: Promoting a pupil who has not learned the material hands them a certificate instead of an education, which is the one thing the school owed them. Repetition joined with real teaching support is the honest response to unmet learning.
Virtue Ethics: Either option can become an institutional shortcut. Passing the pupil onward may avoid a hard teaching problem, while repetition may display severity rather than seriousness. Advancement with substantial support better shows a school willing to remain responsible for the pupil's progress.
Care Ethics: Progression also affects belonging and familiar support. Repetition can separate a pupil from friends and trusted teachers at the moment help is most needed. Keeping the pupil with peers while strengthening support preserves the bonds that may help learning recover.
Sources: OECD (2025), “How do different education systems shape student pathways in primary and lower secondary education?”, Education at a Glance 2025. https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/education-at-a-glance-2025_1c0d9c79-en/full-report/how-do-different-education-systems-shape-student-pathways-in-primary-and-lower-secondary-education_f9f4d15e.html

Title: Suspension or continued attendance
Description: A head teacher faces repeated threats by one pupil toward classmates. Suspension may protect others and signal consequences, but exclusion can deepen disengagement and remove access to support. The head teacher must decide between a temporary suspension and continued attendance under a strict support plan.
Utilitarianism: Repeated threats change the whole classroom climate. Fear disrupts many pupils, while exclusion can deepen one pupil's disengagement. Given repeated threats, a short suspension followed by structured re-entry reduces immediate harm and offers the stronger overall prospect for safety and recovery.
Deontology: Classmates can demand protection from credible threats; the disciplined pupil can demand fair procedure and continued education. Neither claim cancels the other. A proportionate temporary suspension with clear return conditions honours both, provided the evidence is sound.
Virtue Ethics: Authority is tested most when consequences are hard. Excluding the pupil indefinitely would show one failure; ignoring repeated threats would show another. A limited suspension followed by a serious return plan lets authority remain firm without becoming a habit of rejection.
Care Ethics: Sending the pupil away breaks the one set of adult relationships that might change the behaviour, and it does so at the moment those relationships are most needed. Keep the pupil in school, closely held, with the classroom made safe by adults.
Sources: UK Department for Education, “School suspensions and permanent exclusions” statutory guidance. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/school-suspensions-and-permanent-exclusions

Title: Teaching a contested national history
Description: A curriculum committee is revising a textbook about a disputed national event. Several evidence-based accounts may deepen understanding but anger groups seeking one shared story. A single official account is simpler but may suppress legitimate perspectives. The committee must choose plural accounts or one narrative.
Utilitarianism: A textbook shapes understanding far beyond one lesson. Multiple evidence-based accounts strengthen critical thinking and reduce the long-term costs of hiding credible history. Unless plural treatment is likely to trigger severe immediate harm, presenting several supported accounts offers the greater educational and civic benefit.
Deontology: Curriculum choices determine which evidence stays visible. Students are entitled to truthful instruction rather than a politically convenient account. Legitimate disagreement should be presented honestly, with evidence distinguished from propaganda instead of using education to impose conformity on learners.
Virtue Ethics: Contested history tests the habits a curriculum teaches. Choosing one convenient story may make unity easier but weakens intellectual seriousness. A mature curriculum lets uncertainty remain visible and expects students to face difficult evidence without treating every claim as equally sound.
Care Ethics: Public memory enters classrooms through family histories. Different communities may carry loss, pride, or exclusion from the same event. A plural account gives those memories room without humiliating others, helping students remain connected while overlooked voices become harder to erase.
Sources: Council of Europe (2018), “Quality history education in the 21st century: Principles and guidelines.” https://edoc.coe.int/en/teaching-history/7754-quality-history-education-in-the-21st-century-principles-and-guidelines.html

Title: Religious observance in public school
Description: A public school's governing body is reviewing a regular religious observance. Many families value the shared tradition, while pupils of other beliefs may feel pressure even when attendance is optional. Leaders must choose whether to continue the observance or replace it with a nonreligious gathering.
Utilitarianism: A shared gathering affects belonging across the school. Because optional religious observance can still leave minorities exposed, replacing it with a nonreligious gathering is more likely to preserve cohesion while reducing exclusion across the whole school.
Deontology: Religious observance changes the terms of participation. Pupils should not face institutional pressure to participate in worship. If the school cannot make refusal genuinely equal and consequence-free, a nonreligious gathering better respects every pupil's standing.
Virtue Ethics: A school that dissolves an inherited practice at the first sign of discomfort teaches pupils that belonging is disposable. The braver course keeps the observance and does the harder work of making refusal genuinely costless.
Care Ethics: Daily rituals can quietly separate some families. Minority pupils may repeatedly become the ones who leave, refuse, or explain themselves. A common nonreligious gathering removes that social burden while preserving room for faith in relationships where participation is genuinely chosen.
Sources: South African Schools Act 84 of 1996, section 7, religious observances at public schools. https://www.saflii.org/za/legis/consol_act/sasa1996228/

Title: Regulating private tutoring
Description: An education ministry is reviewing paid tutoring outside school. Tutoring can help pupils and provide teachers income, but wealthier families can buy advantages and teachers may pressure their own pupils to pay. The ministry must choose strict limits or broad freedom with basic safeguards.
Utilitarianism: Paid tutoring changes incentives inside ordinary schooling. It can raise achievement for some pupils, yet widen inequality and distort classroom teaching when teachers sell extra help to their own students. Strong limits on conflicts and coercive practices produce the greater system-wide benefit.
Deontology: Private lessons can overlap with public obligations. Teachers should not use authority over existing pupils to create private customers or withhold proper classroom instruction. Regulation may still leave families free to hire independent tutors, preserving legitimate choice without coercion.
Virtue Ethics: Money can alter the teacher-pupil role. When educators profit from needs they are already responsible for addressing, professional judgment becomes entangled with self-interest. Rules should block those arrangements while leaving honest independent tutoring outside the classroom relationship.
Care Ethics: Paid help can reshape classroom trust. A pupil should not wonder whether full attention is reserved for families who can pay after class. Regulation should protect that bond while leaving room for outside tutoring that does not exploit dependence.
Sources: Mark Bray (2009), UNESCO IIEP, “Confronting the shadow education system: what government policies for what private tutoring?” https://www.iiep.unesco.org/en/publication/confronting-shadow-education-system-what-government-policies-what-private-tutoring

Title: Closing an under-enrolled school
Description: A school board is considering closing a small school with falling enrollment. Consolidation would save costs and concentrate staff, but pupils would travel farther and the community would lose a local institution. The board must choose closure or keeping the school open at higher cost.
Utilitarianism: Concentrating teachers and money in fewer buildings gives more pupils better staffed classrooms and specialist subjects a small school cannot sustain. Longer journeys are a real but bounded cost. Closure produces the larger educational gain for the district as a whole.
Deontology: Closure decisions affect access as well as budgets. Public funds must be managed responsibly, but pupils also deserve reasonable access and communities deserve fair consultation. Closing a school is permissible only through transparent criteria that take those claims seriously.
Virtue Ethics: A shrinking school forces uncomfortable public choices. Keeping every building open can turn loyalty into avoidance, while closing by spreadsheet can turn efficiency into indifference. The board's decision should show that it owns both the savings sought and the disruption imposed.
Care Ethics: Distance changes how families remain connected to school. Staff ties and community routines also disappear with closure. Those losses deserve more weight where alternatives are thin, because the affected relationships cannot be recreated by moving resources.
Sources: Ontario Ministry of Education (2015), “Pupil Accommodation Review Guideline.” https://efis.fma.csc.gov.on.ca/faab/Memos/B2015/B9_EN_attach2.pdf

Title: Teacher force allegation
Description: A pupil says a teacher used excessive force during a confrontation. The evidence is unsettled. Removing the teacher from pupil contact protects against possible harm but can damage reputation and disrupt classes. The head teacher must choose temporary removal or continued work with safeguards.
Utilitarianism: Uncertainty makes both action and inaction risky. Another child could be harmed if the allegation is true, while temporary reassignment is reversible if it is false. Moving the teacher away from pupil contact during investigation therefore creates the safer balance of consequences.
Deontology: Two claims arrive before the facts do. The teacher keeps the presumption of innocence and fair process; the children keep their claim to protection from avoidable risk. Temporary reassignment answers both, because a precaution is not a verdict.
Virtue Ethics: Cases like this expose how leaders handle uncertainty. Leaving the teacher untouched may look loyal but can become denial; public punishment before facts are known can become scapegoating. Quiet temporary reassignment shows steadiness without pretending the investigation is already finished.
Care Ethics: Investigation can strain trust on both sides. The pupil needs to know that reporting possible harm does not require immediate contact with the accused teacher, while the teacher remains part of a professional community owed support. Temporary separation protects both relationships.
Sources: UK Department for Education (2025), “Keeping children safe in education 2025,” paras. 383–386 on suspension and alternatives during allegations. https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/68add931969253904d155860/Keeping_children_safe_in_education_from_1_September_2025.pdf

Title: Child withdrawn for household work
Description: A school head learns that a pupil stopped attending because the family needs the child's income. Formal referral may protect education but deepen hardship. Temporary withdrawal reduces pressure but risks permanent dropout. The school must choose referral or temporary acceptance while working with the family.
Utilitarianism: School withdrawal creates immediate and future losses. Keeping a child in work may ease household pressure now but risks lasting educational harm. Formal referral is preferable when it connects the family to support, preserving schooling while reducing the hardship that caused withdrawal.
Deontology: Household need does not erase educational claims. A child's right to schooling cannot be traded away because the family needs income. The school should use proper attendance procedures while public support addresses poverty rather than accepting the loss of education.
Virtue Ethics: Poverty makes simple rule-following morally revealing. Ignoring the withdrawal would let hardship quietly erase a child's future, while rigid enforcement could become hardness toward the family. Formal action joined with practical help proves the school takes both education and poverty seriously.
Care Ethics: A referral turns the school into another authority pressing on a household already stretched, and the child still goes home to that household every night. Better to stay alongside the family, find the income elsewhere, and keep the door open.
Sources: UNICEF Innocenti (2024), “Child Labour and Schooling in Bangladesh: Insights from data and evidence.” https://www.unicef.org/innocenti/reports/child-labour-and-schooling-bangladesh

Title: AI detector and disputed authorship
Description: An instructor suspects an essay was AI-generated after detection software flags it. The student denies this, and the tool can be wrong. Ignoring the flag may miss misconduct; treating it as proof may punish innocent work. The instructor must decide whether stronger evidence is required.
Utilitarianism: A detector flag creates two kinds of error. False accusations can damage grades, trust, and academic standing more severely than one missed misconduct case. Requiring stronger evidence before a formal case therefore minimizes expected harm while preserving a credible route to investigate suspicious work.
Deontology: Suspicion changes a student's standing before proof exists. A detector score may justify questions, but formal accusation requires adequate evidence and a fair chance to respond. Due process protects the student without preventing the instructor from investigating genuine concerns.
Virtue Ethics: Software can make uncertainty look more settled. Treating a score as proof would make the institution less responsible, not more objective. The better academic practice is to investigate, admit uncertainty, and own the final assessment rather than outsource it.
Care Ethics: Academic suspicion enters an existing teaching relationship. The student depends on the instructor to judge work fairly, not merely process a score. Conversation and stronger evidence keep that relationship open while still allowing genuine concerns about authorship to be investigated.
Sources: Weber-Wulff et al. (2023), “Testing of detection tools for AI-generated text,” International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40979-023-00146-z

Title: Remote exam surveillance
Description: A university must supervise an important online exam. Remote proctoring records students at home and flags unusual behavior, which may deter cheating. It also enters private spaces and can misread ordinary movements. Leaders must choose required proctoring or a less intrusive assessment with weaker surveillance.
Utilitarianism: Remote monitoring spreads risk across every examinee. It may deter cheating, but it also creates privacy loss, stress, and false suspicion across the whole cohort. When assessment can be redesigned instead, those broader harms make a less intrusive format the safer net choice.
Deontology: Online assessment still reaches into private space. Students may be required to prove identity and follow examination rules, but surveillance must remain necessary and proportionate. If integrity can be protected another way, excessive recording of students' homes lacks sufficient justification.
Virtue Ethics: Surveillance can become an easy substitute for trust. A university that responds to every risk by watching more closely gradually becomes suspicious by design. Redesigning assessment shows that standards can be protected without allowing technological convenience to define the institution's posture.
Care Ethics: Home is not equally private for everyone. Students may share rooms, live with family, or manage disabilities that make surveillance more intrusive. A less invasive assessment preserves those relationships and keeps human support available when unusual behavior needs explanation.
Sources: Coghlan, Miller & Paterson (2021), “Good Proctor or ‘Big Brother’? Ethics of Online Exam Supervision Technologies,” Philosophy & Technology. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34485025/

Title: Automated scoring of student writing
Description: An assessment provider is considering automated essay scoring. The system is fast and consistent and can reduce marking costs, but it may miss creativity or unusual reasoning that human readers understand. The provider must choose machine-determined scores or automated scoring combined with human judgment.
Utilitarianism: Automated marking trades scale for interpretive limits. It can improve consistency and lower costs, but unreviewed errors may alter educational paths. Combining machine scoring with human review keeps most efficiency gains while reducing costly misjudgments, so the hybrid approach performs best.
Deontology: A score can affect standing without explaining itself. Students are entitled to assessment by relevant criteria and a process that can correct mistakes. Human review preserves accountability when an automated judgment influences educational standing or future opportunities.
Virtue Ethics: Measurement tools can quietly redefine good writing. If evaluators accept only what software recognizes, efficiency begins determining the meaning of quality. Keeping human judgment in the process shows that the provider still accepts responsibility for interpretation and difficult cases.
Care Ethics: Writing still passes from one person to another. A student whose voice or language falls outside the system's patterns needs an actual reader when the score seems wrong. Human review keeps assessment responsive instead of leaving the student with an unanswerable mechanism.
Sources: ETS, “About the e-rater Scoring Engine.” https://www.ets.org/erater/about.html

Title: Student AI use and disclosure
Description: A course permits generative AI for parts of written assignments. The instructor must decide whether students disclose how they used it. Disclosure can clarify authorship but may discourage legitimate assistance and add reporting work. The choice is required disclosure or permitted use without reporting.
Utilitarianism: Detailed reporting on permitted assistance rarely changes what a marker can tell about the work, but it does deter students from using a tool the course already allows. The reporting cost buys little and discourages legitimate use.
Deontology: Permitted assistance still affects what authorship means. A student should not create a false impression about who produced the assessed contribution. When AI materially shapes the submission, acknowledging that assistance is part of honest authorship under clear and consistent rules.
Virtue Ethics: Tool use can shape habits of ownership. Hiding permitted assistance can still train students to avoid responsibility for how work was produced. A brief disclosure keeps AI use connected to intellectual ownership without turning transparency into ritual paperwork.
Care Ethics: Unclear boundaries can make students hide uncertainty. A simple disclosure rule leaves conversation with the instructor open and gives students a safe way to ask what is acceptable. The requirement works best when uncertainty invites guidance rather than punishment.
Sources: University of Auckland, “Advice for students on using Artificial Intelligence.” https://www.auckland.ac.nz/en/students/forms-policies-and-guidelines/student-policies-and-guidelines/academic-integrity-copyright/advice-for-student-on-using-ai.html

Title: Equal access to school-provided AI
Description: A school system is considering giving every pupil access to an approved generative AI tool. Equal access could reduce advantages held by families buying commercial tools, but the system can still make mistakes or unsuitable suggestions. Leaders must choose broad access or continued restriction.
Utilitarianism: School-provided AI changes access and exposure together. A protected tool can spread learning benefits more evenly while reducing reliance on less controlled commercial systems. With safeguards already built in, broad access is likely to create more educational benefit than continued restriction.
Deontology: A school may not hand every pupil a system it knows produces confident falsehoods, however evenly it hands it out. Equal exposure to an unreliable tool is not equal treatment. Access should wait until the school can stand behind it.
Virtue Ethics: New tools test whether adoption is thoughtful. Refusing them simply from fear can become timidity, while distributing them to appear modern makes innovation performative. Guarded access better teaches pupils to question powerful tools rather than either worshipping or avoiding them.
Care Ethics: School access matters most where home access is thin. Pupils without comparable tools depend more heavily on what school provides. Giving them the approved system narrows that gap, but teachers should remain available when the tool confuses or misleads.
Sources: New South Wales Department of Education, “Student use of NSWEduChat.” https://education.nsw.gov.au/schooling/parents-and-carers/artificial-intelligence/student-use-of-nsweduchat

Title: Predictive alerts for struggling students
Description: A university uses activity data to predict who may fail a course. Advisers can contact flagged students early, but predictions can be wrong and students may feel watched or labeled. Leaders must choose whether alerts trigger outreach or support begins only when students ask.
Utilitarianism: Early alerts change when support begins. A respectful message can prevent failure for students who might otherwise remain unnoticed, while a false prediction creates limited harm if no penalty follows. Supportive outreach therefore offers greater overall benefit than waiting for self-referral.
Deontology: Prediction changes how institutions may treat a person. An alert can justify offering help, but it should never restrict opportunities or treat predicted failure as fact. The student remains entitled to privacy, explanation, and freedom to decline support.
Virtue Ethics: Forecasts can tempt advisers to stop judging. Ignoring useful warning signs would be negligent, but treating a score as destiny would make advisers intellectually lazy. Using alerts as questions rather than verdicts keeps judgment active and revisable.
Care Ethics: Outreach can restore contact before failure becomes isolation. Students most in need of help may be least able to ask for it. A personal message can reopen connection, provided advisers listen to the response and do not turn support into monitoring.
Sources: The Open University, “Learning analytics.” https://help.open.ac.uk/index.php/learning-analytics

Title: Legal wage or living wage
Description: A retailer's overseas supplier pays the legal minimum wage, but workers say it does not cover basic living costs. Raising wages would increase prices and might reduce orders or jobs. The buyer must keep the legal rate or require a higher living wage.
Utilitarianism: A wage floor above the local market raises pay for whoever keeps a job and removes the jobs that no longer clear. In a district with few alternatives, the orders themselves are the benefit. Keep the legal rate and expand the order book.
Deontology: Legal compliance is not the whole obligation when a company knowingly relies on wages too low for basic needs. Workers must not be used merely as cheap inputs. The buyer should require pay compatible with decent subsistence and safe employment.
Virtue Ethics: A firm shows what it thinks workers are worth through the conditions it is willing to purchase. Hiding behind the legal minimum makes compliance a ceiling on responsibility. Requiring better pay makes the supply relationship less dependent on convenient poverty.
Care Ethics: These wages enter particular households as rent, food, medicine, and school costs. Walking away from the supplier could also remove that income completely. A responsible buyer should raise pay gradually while keeping orders stable enough to protect those families.
Sources: Werner A, Lim M. (2016), “The Ethics of the Living Wage: A Review and Research Agenda,” Journal of Business Ethics. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10551-015-2562-z

Title: Child labor at a supplier
Description: A brand discovers that a supplier employs children whose families depend on their wages. Ending the contract would remove the children from this factory but may push them into worse work. The buyer must terminate immediately or fund remediation while continuing the contract.
Utilitarianism: Immediate termination cleans the buyer's supply chain but may leave the children poorer and less safe. Keeping the supplier temporarily while funding school access and replacement family income addresses the harm without removing livelihood. Remediation leaves fewer people worse off.
Deontology: Children have a claim not to be used in prohibited labor, and commercial benefit cannot excuse that violation. The buyer may continue only as part of a verified remediation plan that ends the work promptly. An ordinary business relationship cannot continue unchanged.
Virtue Ethics: A company can protect its reputation faster than it can protect a child. Cutting the supplier loose may display purity while exporting the problem elsewhere. Staying long enough to repair the situation makes responsibility more than distancing the brand from blame.
Care Ethics: The child is connected to parents, siblings, school, and the income that keeps the household functioning. Removing one harmful relationship without replacing what it provided can deepen another harm. Remediation should keep the family supported while the child leaves work.
Sources: International Labour Organization (2021), “Supplier guidance on preventing, identifying and addressing child labour.” https://www.ilo.org/publications/supplier-guidance-preventing-identifying-and-addressing-child-labour

Title: Defect in an implanted device
Description: A medical-device maker finds a small failure risk in an implanted product already used by patients. Warning everyone may trigger risky removal surgeries, while silence denies patients information about their own bodies. Executives must notify all affected patients or monitor quietly through physicians.
Utilitarianism: Notifying everyone converts a small failure risk into thousands of explant operations, each carrying its own surgical mortality. The removals will kill more people than the defect does. Monitor through physicians and warn only where risk is concentrated.
Deontology: Patients carrying the device are entitled to material information needed for decisions about their own bodies. The manufacturer cannot withhold a known defect because disclosure may produce difficult choices. Notify patients through their clinicians and let informed individuals decide what follows.
Virtue Ethics: A defect tests whether the manufacturer sees uncertainty as a reason for candor or concealment. Quiet monitoring protects the company from alarm as much as patients from surgery. Open risk communication accepts that trust requires sharing bad information before certainty arrives.
Care Ethics: Each patient lives differently with the implanted device, and a population-wide recall cannot capture those differences. Clinicians should contact patients personally, explain both failure and surgery risks, and remain available afterward. The relationship must carry the uncertainty rather than secrecy.
Sources: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, “What is a Medical Device Recall?” https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/medical-device-recalls-and-early-alerts/what-medical-device-recall

Title: Customer encryption and lawful access
Description: A technology company sells encrypted devices that even the company cannot unlock. Investigators present a lawful order seeking access to one serious criminal case. Building special access could help the investigation but create a method others may exploit. Executives must build access or refuse.
Utilitarianism: One investigation may prevent serious harm, yet a reusable access method can weaken security for millions of ordinary users and future targets. Because that vulnerability scales beyond this case, refusing to create it produces the safer overall consequences despite the investigative loss.
Deontology: A lawful order creates a serious obligation to assist legitimate investigation, but it does not automatically require creating a new capability that compromises other customers' security. The company should comply with information it possesses while refusing to manufacture a general vulnerability.
Virtue Ethics: The company promised security before the difficult case arrived. Creating an exceptional weakness under pressure would show that promise lasts only until keeping it becomes costly. Refusal demonstrates constancy of purpose, provided leaders also cooperate fully through methods that do not undermine the product.
Care Ethics: The victim of the investigated crime deserves help, while millions of customers depend on the same encryption for safety from abuse, theft, and surveillance. The company should support investigators through other evidence without changing a protective relationship relied on by everyone else.
Sources: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2018), “Decrypting the Encryption Debate: A Framework for Decision Makers.” https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/25010

Title: Pricing a breakthrough medicine
Description: A pharmaceutical company owns a newly approved treatment that can transform a serious illness. A very high price would fund investors and future research but leave many patients without access. The board must choose a premium price or a lower price that expands treatment.
Utilitarianism: Today's patients are visible and tomorrow's are not, but the pipeline is paid for out of prices like this one. A premium price on one treatment funds the treatments that do not yet exist. Set the price high and licence generically later.
Deontology: A patent grants control over the medicine, not permission to exploit desperate need without limit. Patients remain persons with serious claims to access, while investors also have legitimate contractual interests. The company should set a fair sustainable price rather than maximize what illness permits.
Virtue Ethics: Scarcity of a cure can make market power feel like ordinary pricing power. A company that extracts the maximum from desperation becomes shaped by that choice. Charging less while remaining viable shows commercial success need not depend on testing how much suffering can bear.
Care Ethics: The medicine reaches the company as revenue but reaches patients as time, health, and continued family life. Pricing should begin from those dependent on treatment, including people without strong insurance or wealth. A lower sustainable price keeps that relationship from becoming exclusion.
Sources: Parker-Lue S, Santoro M, Koski G. (2015), “The Ethics and Economics of Pharmaceutical Pricing,” Annual Review of Pharmacology and Toxicology. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25149920/

Title: Classifying platform drivers
Description: A ride platform controls fares, ratings, and access to customers, while drivers choose when to log in and use their own cars. Employee status would bring protections but raise costs and reduce flexibility. The company must classify drivers as employees or independent contractors.
Utilitarianism: Contractor status preserves flexible entry and may keep prices lower, but workers can carry accident, illness, and income risks the platform helps create. Given the company's control over core terms, employee status better distributes those costs and produces more secure overall welfare.
Deontology: Classification should follow the real relationship rather than whichever label costs the company less. When the platform controls essential terms of work, it assumes corresponding obligations toward those performing it. Drivers should receive employee protections if the substance of the relationship is employment.
Virtue Ethics: Calling workers independent while controlling price, access, and discipline lets the company keep authority without acknowledging what authority makes it. An institution that names the relationship honestly is less likely to build its business on responsibility shifted downward.
Care Ethics: A driver absorbs fuel, injury, illness, and unstable demand personally while the platform organizes the work around them. Employment protections keep those risks from falling entirely on households that depend on each week's earnings, even if some scheduling flexibility is reduced.
Sources: International Labour Organization (2021), “The role of digital labour platforms in transforming the world of work.” https://www.ilo.org/publications/flagship-reports/role-digital-labour-platforms-transforming-world-work

Title: Choosing a ship recycling yard
Description: A shipping company must retire an old vessel. A cheaper recycling yard provides many local jobs but has weaker worker protections and hazardous conditions. A certified safer yard costs more and reduces the sale value. Executives must choose the cheaper yard or safer facility.
Utilitarianism: The cheaper yard supports employment and recycles valuable material, but severe injuries and toxic exposure impose costs workers cannot easily avoid. Paying more for a safer facility preserves the recycling benefit while reducing concentrated harm. The company should choose the safer yard.
Deontology: Selling the vessel does not end responsibility for foreseeable conditions under which it will be dismantled. Workers may need the job, but that need cannot make avoidable danger acceptable. The company should contract with a facility that meets credible safety standards.
Virtue Ethics: The last owner decides whether responsibility ends when the ship leaves its books. Choosing the lowest bidder while knowing how the savings are produced makes distance a moral excuse. Paying for safer recycling keeps stewardship attached to the asset until its end.
Care Ethics: The men at the cheaper yard are not an abstraction either, and the ship leaving takes their work with it. Standards written far away are enforced on people who were not asked. Send it there, and pay for the equipment they lack.
Sources: International Labour Organization (2004), “Safety and health in shipbreaking: Guidelines for Asian countries and Turkey.” https://www.ilo.org/publications/safety-and-health-shipbreaking-guidelines-asian-countries-and-turkey

Title: Microfinance growth and poorer borrowers
Description: A microfinance lender can attract commercial funding by making larger loans to safer, better-off borrowers. That strategy would expand the institution and stabilize finances but leave fewer resources for poorer clients it was created to serve. Leaders must pursue growth or preserve poorer outreach.
Utilitarianism: Commercial growth can fund more lending overall, and larger reliable loans may subsidize smaller ones. If expansion genuinely increases the number of poor borrowers ultimately served, accepting commercial capital is worthwhile. Growth should proceed with a measurable floor protecting poorer outreach.
Deontology: The institution was entrusted with a stated purpose of serving people excluded from ordinary finance. Quietly replacing them with safer customers while keeping the social mission in public language breaks that commitment. Growth is permissible only if the original beneficiaries remain substantively included.
Virtue Ethics: Mission drift often begins without anyone announcing a new mission. Targets, incentives, and easier clients slowly redefine what success means. Leaders should notice that change before profitability becomes the institution's identity and preserve practices that keep difficult borrowers visible.
Care Ethics: Poorer borrowers are precisely the people with the fewest alternative lenders when this institution moves upward. Growth that leaves them behind breaks a relationship built around exclusion from mainstream finance. Expansion should be structured so their access does not become the sacrifice.
Sources: Maîtrot M. (2019), “Understanding Social Performance: A ‘Practice Drift’ at the Frontline of Microfinance Institutions in Bangladesh,” Development and Change. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/dech.12398

Title: Marketing infant formula safely
Description: A formula producer wants to expand sales where many families lack reliable clean water and health information. Advertising may help parents who need substitutes find a product, but aggressive promotion can displace safer breastfeeding. Managers must market broadly or restrict promotion to health-guided channels.
Utilitarianism: Formula is essential for some infants, but broad promotion can change feeding choices far beyond those cases and increase infection where preparation is unsafe. Restricting promotion while keeping the product available through reliable health information prevents more harm across families.
Deontology: Parents are entitled to accurate information rather than persuasion that exploits uncertainty about infant feeding. The company may sell a lawful substitute, but it should not manipulate caregivers into abandoning safer options without informed reasons. Promotion should be restricted and factual.
Virtue Ethics: A market opportunity becomes revealing when customers cannot easily evaluate the risk attached to increased consumption. A company that moderates its own promotion refuses to turn informational advantage into sales pressure. Restraint here protects the difference between serving demand and manufacturing it.
Care Ethics: An infant depends entirely on the caregiver's feeding decision and on whether safe preparation is actually possible at home. Marketing should support that bond with clear guidance, not add pressure. Promotion belongs where families can receive help choosing and using substitutes safely.
Sources: World Health Organization (2024), “Marketing of breast-milk substitutes: national implementation of the international code, status report 2024.” https://www.who.int/publications/b/74180

Title: Sales targets and customer consent
Description: A bank's ambitious sales targets have increased revenue, but complaints show some employees opening products customers did not clearly request. Lowering targets may slow growth and reduce bonuses. Senior leaders must keep the targets with tighter monitoring or reduce them and accept lower sales.
Utilitarianism: High targets create real revenue, yet even a small rate of unauthorized sales can spread fees, complaints, remediation costs, and mistrust across many customers. Reducing the targets removes the incentive at its source and is likely to produce the better long-term outcome.
Deontology: Customer consent is not a performance variable that may be traded against growth. Management must design incentives that do not pressure employees to obtain products without genuine authorization. Targets should be reduced when the system predictably undermines that basic requirement.
Virtue Ethics: Targets teach employees what leadership actually rewards. If managers praise numbers while treating complaints as an implementation problem, the institution becomes fluent in looking away. Lowering the targets admits that growth achieved through compromised consent is not success worth keeping.
Care Ethics: Frontline employees and customers meet inside the pressure created by senior management. Extreme targets can make workers fear missing quotas and customers absorb the result. Reducing the pressure protects both sides of that relationship instead of asking monitoring to repair it afterward.
Sources: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (2016), “CFPB Warns Financial Companies About Sales and Production Incentives That May Lead to Fraud or Consumer Abuse.” https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/newsroom/cfpb-warns-financial-companies-about-sales-and-production-incentives-may-lead-fraud-or-consumer-abuse/

Title: Automation and workforce layoffs
Description: A manufacturer can automate a large part of production and remain competitive, but many long-serving workers would lose their jobs. Delaying automation protects employment for now but raises the risk the whole plant later becomes uncompetitive. Executives must automate quickly or phase the change.
Utilitarianism: Rapid automation may preserve the company yet concentrate severe losses on workers and the surrounding economy. A phased transition with retraining captures much of the productivity gain while giving people time to move. Unless delay threatens survival, phasing distributes the loss more tolerably.
Deontology: Workers are not guaranteed permanent jobs, and management may adopt productive technology when business conditions require it. But long service creates obligations of fair notice and honest transition. Automation is permissible if layoffs follow transparent terms rather than treating people as disposable costs.
Virtue Ethics: Loyalty that keeps people in work the firm cannot sustain is sentimentality wearing gratitude's clothes, and it ends with everyone losing the job at once. The honest course is to move quickly, say so plainly, and pay generously on the way out.
Care Ethics: The lost job may also be a mortgage payment, school fee, medical coverage, and community role. A phased transition gives families time to reorganize those dependencies. The company should automate in a way that does not make workers carry the whole adjustment overnight.
Sources: Acemoglu D, Restrepo P. (2020), “Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets,” Journal of Political Economy. https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/705716

Title: Aggressive corporate tax planning
Description: A multinational can legally shift profits through low-tax jurisdictions and greatly reduce its tax bill. The savings benefit shareholders and investment, but the company still depends on public infrastructure and services where it operates. Directors must use the structure or pay more locally.
Utilitarianism: Lower taxes can finance investment, wages, and lower prices, but widespread aggressive avoidance weakens public services and shifts burdens to others. Because the strategy depends on rules working differently for this firm than for the system as a whole, directors should reject it.
Deontology: Directors are stewards of money belonging to others, and paying more tax than the law requires spends it on a preference the owners never agreed to. The remedy for a rule that permits too much is to change the rule, not to disobey it.
Virtue Ethics: A firm can obey every sentence of a statute while teaching itself to ask only how little contribution is unavoidable. That habit turns cleverness into evasion. Paying a reasonable share reflects an institution willing to belong to the society from which it profits.
Care Ethics: Tax savings appear on corporate accounts; reduced public revenue appears in schools, transport, clinics, and services used by workers and communities around the business. Directors should not treat those shared supports as someone else's responsibility while continuing to depend on them.
Sources: Lenz H. (2020), “Aggressive Tax Avoidance by Managers of Multinational Companies as a Violation of Their Moral Duty to Obey the Law: A Kantian Rationale,” Journal of Business Ethics. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10551-018-4087-8

Title: High-risk mortgage lending
Description: A lender can approve mortgages with low initial payments for borrowers who cannot afford the later full rate unless income rises. The loans expand home access and generate profit, but defaults could cause foreclosure. Managers must offer the loans or require affordable long-term payments.
Utilitarianism: Some borrowers gain homes they would otherwise miss, but loans designed around hoped-for future income create predictable foreclosure risk for households and neighborhoods. Requiring payments borrowers can sustain sacrifices some approvals now while preventing larger downstream losses. Use the safer standard.
Deontology: A lender may charge for risk, but it must not present a loan as affordable when the contract is structured around payments the borrower is unlikely to meet. Fair dealing requires terms customers can understand and a genuine assessment of repayment ability.
Virtue Ethics: Selling a loan that works only if everything goes right turns optimism into a sales tool. A lender that earns today while leaving tomorrow's failure with the borrower practices cleverness without judgment. Sustainable underwriting is a better measure of responsible enterprise.
Care Ethics: Foreclosure reaches children, partners, neighbors, and local stability long after the original signature. The borrower may desperately want the house, but that desire should not be used against them. Lending should support a home that the household can realistically keep.
Sources: Watkins JP. (2011), “Banking Ethics and the Goldman Rule,” Journal of Economic Issues 45(2). https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.2753/JEI0021-3624450213

Title: Emergency pricing during a shortage
Description: After a disaster, a retailer has few generators left. Wholesalers can send more quickly if the retailer accepts higher replacement costs. Raising prices could fund restocking and discourage hoarding, but poorer families may be shut out. Managers must raise prices or ration at near-normal prices.
Utilitarianism: Higher prices can discourage hoarding and draw replacement stock into the damaged area faster, increasing the number of generators eventually available. Because supply responds to the price signal here, raising prices is likely to help more households overall than fixed-price rationing.
