Deontology: People facing an emergency should not become a captive market simply because demand suddenly exceeds supply. The retailer may recover genuine higher costs, but using desperation to extract whatever buyers will pay fails fair dealing. Keep prices near normal and ration fairly.
Virtue Ethics: A crisis reveals whether pricing is treated as allocation or opportunity. Refusing every increase may slow restocking, while exploiting panic makes need itself profitable. A restrained retailer keeps prices close to ordinary levels and uses rationing rather than turning scarcity into windfall revenue.
Care Ethics: The customer unable to pay the new price may be caring for children, an older relative, or someone dependent on electricity for safety. Rationing lets limited stock reach more households without deciding access by wealth. Keep prices near normal.
Sources: Snyder J. (2009), “What’s the Matter with Price Gouging?” Business Ethics Quarterly 19(2). https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/business-ethics-quarterly/article/abs/whats-the-matter-with-price-gouging/79B4985901C7D78C215219124C000B69

Title: Polluting plant and local jobs
Description: A factory is the largest employer in its town but repeatedly pollutes a nearby river. Installing full controls would make the plant unprofitable, while closure would remove many livelihoods. The owner must keep operating with partial controls or close until cleaner production is viable.
Utilitarianism: Closure protects health and the river but can impose immediate unemployment across an entire town. If partial controls materially reduce pollution while keeping the plant alive, continued operation during a fixed transition period creates less total harm than abrupt shutdown.
Deontology: Employment does not give a company permission to impose unconsented pollution on neighbors who bear the health and environmental costs. If safe operation cannot be achieved, the owner must stop production rather than make one community the involuntary price of other people's jobs.
Virtue Ethics: A business becomes irresponsible when it treats jobs as a shield against correcting damage it causes. Yet closing overnight can also abandon the people who built the plant. A credible transition toward cleaner production avoids both excuses: pollution and disposable employment.
Care Ethics: Workers and riverside families are not separate stakeholder lists; they may be the same households. Closing the plant protects health while threatening income. A timed transition with wage support and pollution reduction keeps responsibility connected to both forms of dependence.
Sources: Hasan MN, Uba C. (2026), “Shifting harm without solving it: The socio-political dynamics of industrial relocation failure in Bangladesh’s tannery industry,” Environment and Planning C. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/23996544261444714

Title: Recall before anyone is injured
Description: A manufacturer learns that a household product has a defect that could rarely cause serious injury, although no injuries have been reported. A full recall would be expensive and discard many safe units. Executives must recall now or investigate further while sales continue.
Utilitarianism: The defect is rare, but the potential injury is serious and continued sales increase the number of exposed households. A temporary stop and recall of affected batches prevents irreversible harm at a cost spread across the company. Recall now and investigate simultaneously.
Deontology: Customers were sold a product on the understanding that known serious hazards would not be concealed from them. The absence of reported injury does not remove that obligation. Distribution should stop, the defect should be reported, and affected customers should be informed.
Virtue Ethics: Waiting for the first injured customer would make harm the evidence needed to justify responsibility. A manufacturer that acts before a casualty accepts uncertainty in the direction of safety rather than revenue. That is what ownership of a product should mean.
Care Ethics: The person who encounters the rare defect will bear nearly all of the consequence while the company spreads recall cost across millions of sales. Acting early stops that unequal burden from falling on an unknown household simply because no one has been hurt yet.
Sources: U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, “Duty to Report to CPSC: Rights and Responsibilities of Businesses.” https://www.cpsc.gov/Business--Manufacturing/Recall-Guidance/Duty-to-Report-to-CPSC-Rights-and-Responsibilities-of-Businesses

Title: Closing the last local branch
Description: A bank's last branch in a small town is losing money as customers move online. Closing it would cut costs, but older residents and small businesses still rely on in-person services. Executives must close the branch or keep it open despite losses.
Utilitarianism: Keeping one lightly used branch permanently may consume resources that serve more customers elsewhere, but closure imposes unusually high costs on people with few substitutes. A smaller branch with reduced hours preserves essential access while limiting losses. Do not close completely.
Deontology: A bank is not required to operate every unprofitable location indefinitely. If accounts remain accessible through reasonable alternatives and contractual services continue, closure can be permissible. The company must give fair notice and ensure customers can retrieve funds and records without obstruction.
Virtue Ethics: Efficiency can become an excuse for forgetting why a branch existed in the first place. Leaving the town only after digital customers make everyone else uneconomic would show a narrow idea of service. Reducing hours is a better form of practical stewardship.
Care Ethics: For a customer who cannot drive or use online banking confidently, the branch is not a convenience but the relationship through which money remains usable. Keeping some staffed access preserves that dependence without requiring the bank to maintain the full old operation.
Sources: Federal Reserve Board (2019), “Perspectives from Main Street: Bank Branch Access in Rural Communities.” https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/november-2019-bank-branch-access-in-rural-communities.htm

Title: Paying small suppliers first
Description: A large company has a temporary cash shortage and cannot pay every supplier on time. Paying strictly by due date is predictable, but several small suppliers may fail if delayed. The finance chief must follow invoice order or prioritize smaller suppliers facing collapse.
Utilitarianism: A short delay costs every supplier something, but insolvency at a small firm can destroy jobs and future supply capacity while a larger vendor survives the same delay. Prioritizing the most fragile suppliers prevents the greater total loss during this temporary shortage.
Deontology: Suppliers delivered goods under agreed payment terms and are entitled to performance according to those commitments. The company cannot rewrite priority after receiving the benefit simply because some creditors appear stronger. Pay according to contractual due dates unless suppliers voluntarily agree otherwise.
Virtue Ethics: Cash pressure exposes whether the company treats suppliers as partners or as financing it can take without consent. Protecting smaller firms may be defensible, but secretly moving others down the queue is not. Leaders should negotiate openly rather than improvise private fairness.
Care Ethics: A delayed invoice at a small supplier can become missed wages the same week, while a large vendor may have credit lines and reserves. Priority should follow where payment sustains the most dependent business ties, accompanied by direct explanation to those waiting.
Sources: OECD (2019), “Financing SMEs and Entrepreneurs 2019,” section on payment delays and SME survival. https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/financing-smes-and-entrepreneurs-2019_fin_sme_ent-2019-en/full-report/component-7.html

Title: Takeover premium and planned layoffs
Description: A company's board receives a takeover offer far above the current share price. The buyer plans to combine operations and eliminate many local jobs, while rejecting the offer may leave shareholders with less value. Directors must accept the premium or remain independent.
Utilitarianism: Shareholders gain immediately from the premium, but large layoffs can reduce household income, local spending, and valuable firm knowledge after the merger. When the company is healthy without the deal, those wider losses can outweigh the premium. The board should reject it.
Deontology: Directors hold formal responsibilities toward the corporation and its shareholders, while employees also have contractual rights that must be honored. If the governing rules require serious consideration of the superior offer, directors cannot reject it merely to preserve existing jobs.
Virtue Ethics: A board that treats the highest bid as the complete meaning of stewardship reduces a living institution to its sale price. Refusing a lucrative offer can be justified when independence protects work, knowledge, and commitments the company has deliberately built.
Care Ethics: The premium is distributed to owners, while job losses arrive in particular households and communities that cannot diversify the shock. Directors should consider those relationships before accepting. If the company can remain viable alone, preserving them weighs heavily against the sale.
Sources: Krishnan HA, Hitt MA, Park D. (2007), “Acquisition Premiums, Subsequent Workforce Reductions and Post-Acquisition Performance,” Journal of Management Studies. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-6486.2006.00672.x

Title: Enforcing a worker noncompete
Description: A company funded specialized training for an employee who now wants to join a direct competitor. A signed noncompete blocks the move for a year and protects the firm's investment, but limits the worker's career. Executives must enforce the clause or release the employee.
Utilitarianism: Enforcement may encourage firms to invest in training, but restricting mobility also suppresses wages, knowledge diffusion, and better job matches across the market. Unless the employee holds genuinely sensitive information, releasing them creates broader economic benefit than protecting this training investment.
Deontology: The employee knowingly accepted training under a contract containing the restriction, and the company spent money in reliance on that agreement. If the clause is proportionate and lawful, keeping the promise matters. The firm may enforce it rather than absorb the entire bargain.
Virtue Ethics: Training someone and then treating their improved ability as property confuses investment with ownership of a person. A confident firm protects real secrets but does not fear every departure. Releasing the employee proves that developing people was not merely a way to bind them.
Care Ethics: A year outside the worker's field can affect income, family plans, and an entire career trajectory, while the company can protect specific confidential information separately. Releasing the clause keeps the employment relationship from reaching beyond departure farther than genuine trust requires.
Sources: Andrews D, Garnero A. (2025), “Five facts on non-compete and related clauses in OECD countries,” OECD Economics Department Working Papers No. 1833. https://doi.org/10.1787/727da13e-en
